articles.title: 2026 Subaru Outback Limited review: Boxy outside, almost premium inside
articles.text:
When station wagons headed for the same retirement home as the vinyl roof and the opera window, Subaru looked at its sensible Legacy wagon and had a different idea. Raise it a few inches, wrap the lower body in plastic cladding, name it for the Australian bush, and suburban families would drive to soccer practice while imagining themselves fording streams and climbing sand dunes.
In giving birth to the Legacy Outback in 1995, Subaru more or less created the template for the modern, adventure-minded, off-road-themed crossover. By the 2000 model year, the Outback had graduated from trim level to standalone model, and it has been paying the bulk of Subaru’s bills ever since.
Today, the 2026 Outback marks a new era in the model’s history. The wagon silhouette that defined six generations has given way to a sharpened two-box shape that’s much more at home parked next to an upright Forester or Ascent. Tall, square, and profusely SUV-like, the new edition won’t win any beauty contests, but form follows function more than ever in the Outback.
More crossover than wagon, the new Subaru Outback is not the best it has ever looked, at least as far as the exterior is concerned.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
More crossover than wagon, the new Subaru Outback is not the best it has ever looked, at least as far as the exterior is concerned.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
Standard all-wheel drive across all six trim levels (starting at about $36,000 to just under $49,000, including the required $1,450 destination) ensures all Outbacks have similar poor-weather and poor-road ability, though the Wilderness version rides 0.8 inches (20 mm) higher off the ground and comes with more dedicated all-terrain tires. My Limited test vehicle stickered at $43,165.
Much improved interior
The new Outback isn’t pretty, but spend a week driving it, as I did, and you’ll quickly care less about the outer skin than the inner capability. The extra height over the 2025 version affords much improved passenger and cargo room. There’s one caveat, though: The new interior steps threateningly close to premium quality, and a new infotainment system and electronics package pull everyday usability and convenience up the ladder by a rung or two.
Climb in and close the door, and you’ll find the dashboard cleaner than before, with climate controls thankfully presented as tangible knobs and buttons rather than the sometimes-lethargic digital renderings of the prior Outback. The only demerit here is the mesh fabric covering the upper door panels and part of the dashboard. This material looks a bit cheap and can be pulled like a shirt, making the pattern askew.
The new interior is an improvement.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
The new interior is an improvement.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
While the front seats offer lots of legroom and adjustability and are very comfortable even on multi-hour drives, the rear seat offers even more space and shoulder room. But the seatbacks do not recline, as in many SUVs. Ingress and egress from both front and rear seats is also excellent. The Limited trim includes heated outboard rear seats. Thoughtful shopping bag hooks and tie-downs in the cargo area come standard, and there’s also meaningful under-floor storage back there, too.
On the technology front, a new 12.1-inch infotainment system responds quicker and proves easier to navigate, with large, highly legible icons. You can also more easily read the new 12.3-inch, hi-res, and configurable digital instrument cluster. Several USB-A and USB-C ports come standard front and rear, and there’s wireless charging up front.
My Outback Limited’s Harman Kardon audio system (12 speakers, 576 watts) reproduced sound better than I anticipated, whether I was piping in Miles Davis, MC5, or Mahler. The top Touring trims include a hands-free highway driving system that bridges the adaptive cruise control and lane-centering already aboard the Limited test vehicle.
ADAS needs work
A few words about active driving assists. Though the generous list of standard lane-keeping, lane-centering, and adaptive cruise features worked well, it was hard to appreciate them because the DriverFocus Distraction Mitigation system’s functions were so overbearing. Look away from the road dead-ahead for more than a second—even to glance at the infotainment screen—and you get an electronic finger-wagging that you’re not paying attention.
Go here to tweak the advanced driver assistance systems.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
Go here to tweak the advanced driver assistance systems.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
With lane-centering and adaptive cruise engaged, the Outback repeatedly scolded me to put my hands on the steering wheel—when my hands were on the steering wheel. And then, when I intentionally let go to try to wake the system up and re-gripped the wheel with the firmness of a General Patton handshake, the system took about five seconds to register the re-grip.
Of course, you can disable the DriverFocus system, but you’d need to disable it on every restart of the car. Yes, Subaru laudably has put safety at the forefront, but I gave up driving with my mother 40 years ago.
Underneath the new boxy sheetmetal, Subaru avoids reinventing what already worked. The test Limited’s standard 2.5 L flat-four-cylinder engine develops 180 hp (134 kW) and 178 lb-ft (241 Nm) of torque. That’s adequate oomph, but it’s hardly brisk when toting around the Outback Limited’s 3,741 lbs (1,697 kg).
The turbocharged 2.4 L engine of the XT versions, making 260 hp (194 kW) and 277 lb-ft (376 Nm) of torque, offers power that the base engine can only dream of (if engines could dream). No hybrid version is available yet, but I suspect a hybrid Outback will arrive for 2027, likely with a version of the 194 hp (145 kW) drivetrain currently used in the Forester Hybrid. For those looking for something entirely electric, the new Subaru Trailseeker is marketed in other regions as the E-Outback and is close to, if not identical in, dimensions.
Both engines pair with Subaru’s continuously variable transmission, which performs adequately in sedate, everyday driving but lurches when pushed and can elicit some droning when climbing long freeway grades and accelerating hard.
For now, there’s a choice of two engines.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
For now, there’s a choice of two engines.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
Behind the wheel
More impressive is how much more refined the new Outback feels when not asked to perform like a sports car. The Outback hushes wind noise, smooths bumps and harshness on the freeway, and seems to dispatch dirt road roughness with nearly the same ease as it does on the highway. Twisty back roads are not really on the menu. I’d save that for the BR-Zs and WRXs of the world.
Though no off-road match for a Jeep Wrangler, the new Outback does everything the prior generation did when the road ends, meaning quite a lot given natural limitations. Both old and new Outbacks provide the same 8.7 inches (221 mm) of ground clearance (though the new Wilderness version yields 9.5 inches/241 mm).
Various traction-seeking features come standard on the Limited, like X-Mode Traction Management, which softens the throttle opening to avoid an initial loss of traction; variable torque split, which apportions more or less power to the wheels with more traction; and hill descent control, which regulates downhill speed so the driver can focus on steering on slippery downslopes. In addition to extra ground clearance and knobbier all-terrain tires, the Outback Wilderness adds selectable snow/dirt and deep snow/mud settings to the X-Mode system.
Thankfully, it’s not an all touchscreen interface. There are plenty of buttons.
Jim Resnick
Thankfully, it’s not an all touchscreen interface. There are plenty of buttons.
Jim Resnick
The back seat has decent legroom.
Jim Resnick
The back seat has decent legroom.
Jim Resnick
Not quite class-leading, but more convenient to load than the Honda Passport.
Jim Resnick
Not quite class-leading, but more convenient to load than the Honda Passport.
Jim Resnick
The back seat has decent legroom.
Jim Resnick
Not quite class-leading, but more convenient to load than the Honda Passport.
Jim Resnick
Regardless of traction-seeking software and hardware, I found the Outback Limited capable of handling anything I threw at it on the off-road trails I use in Arizona, within reason. Cliff-climbing and bouldering are clearly out of the question for the Outback, and like an athlete getting on in years, you have to be aware of your vehicle’s limitations before committing to off-road heroism. Your oil pan, ball joints, and differentials will thank you.
The Outback offers 34.6 cubic feet (980 L) of cargo space behind the rear seats and 80.5 cu. ft. (2,280 L) with rear seats folded. That’s a bit lower than class cargo leaders like the enormous way-back in Honda’s Passport, but the Outback is no slouch. Plus, the Outback benefits from a lower rear load-in height, so lugging heavy objects inside will prove easier.
There’s storage aplenty for small items, including carpeted space in each door pocket for a big 32-ounce water bottle, plus various little pockets around the interior for other trinkets. The center console isn’t huge, but it’s quite deep.
The EPA rates the Outback Limited’s fuel economy at 25/31/27 mpg in city/highway/combined driving (9.4/7.6/8.7 L/100 km). In my own mix of suburban and highway driving, I saw 28.4 mpg (8.3 L/100 km) over a week, discounting the off-roading session; that sort of driving is not comparable with normal driving or economy ratings. The Outback can also tow up to 3,500 lbs (1,588 kg), sufficient to pull a small trailer or boat.
Still not a looker, though.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
Still not a looker, though.
Credit:
Jim Resnick
While the new Outback’s styling will likely spark the loudest debates, after a week in the driver’s seat, it’s clear that Subaru has kept the vehicle’s mission intact. The latest Outback remains faithful to its well-established raison d’être as a tool for navigating your automotive life, be it in the carpool lane during rush hour or riding along the spine of the Continental Divide at sunrise.
A veteran of journalism, product planning and communications in the automotive and music space, Jim reports, critiques and lectures on autos, music and culture.

articles.title: YouTube now requires creators to have twice as many watch hours to start earning money | TechCrunch
articles.text:
YouTube announced on Monday that new creators will have to meet higher thresholds to begin earning money from ads and subscriptions.
Creators who want to start earning on the platform will need at least 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. Currently, creators need 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours over the past year or 1,000 subscribers and 10 million Shorts views over the past 90 days.
The change is going into effect starting February 1. The Google-owned company says the update won’t impact creators already in the YouTube Partner Program.
Additionally, YouTube announced that creators will need to maintain 10 million Shorts views over a 90-day period to earn money through the Shorts Creators Pool. Channels below this threshold will remain in the partner program and continue earning on long-form content, with Shorts revenue resuming once they cross 10 million views again.
YouTube says the changes are being introduced to “keep pace with the growth of YouTube, which now sees over 200 billion daily Shorts views and over a billion hours of watch time on TV” every day.
The changes make it harder for creators to enter and remain in YouTube’s monetization program, especially for Shorts creators. By increasing thresholds, YouTube is putting more pressure on creators’ ability to consistently bring in large audiences before being able to earn money on the platform, which could in turn lead to fewer new entrants being able to monetize their content.
As part of Monday’s announcement, YouTube announced that it’s expanding its more affordable Premium Lite subscription to all countries where YouTube Premium is available. Creators receive a share of subscription revenue based on member watch time and views, with 55% going to long-form video creators and 45% to Shorts creators.
“With these additional subscribers, creators can expect higher earnings: when a user signs up for Premium, partners, on average, earn more than when the user was watching ads,” the company wrote in the blog post.
Premium Lite offers an ad-free experience on most videos, along with the ability to download videos for offline viewing and play videos in the background.
YouTube isn’t the only social media company revising its creator rewards programs. Over the weekend, Elon Musk’s X also revamped creator payouts by changing its guidelines to only reward original content. Earlier this spring, Facebook also launched a new monetization program to attract creators from TikTok and YouTube.

articles.title: CATL y BYD coinciden en que ninguna quiere ser la segunda en probar las baterías de estado sólido en coches. Y ya apuntan a 2027
articles.text:
Los grandes fabricantes de baterías del mundo ya preparan sus hojas de ruta para el desarrollo y entrada en producción de nuevas químicas que ofrezcan mayor densidad energética y autonomía. Hay una evolución constante en ello y los vehículos eléctricos son los que más se van a beneficiar de este cambio.
En el caso de CATL, que basicamente es el mayor fabricante de baterías del mundo en cuanto a cuota de mercado, ha confirmado que comenzará una producción piloto a pequeña escala de celdas de estado sólido en 2027. Y curiosamente, esa fecha coincide con el calendario que ya había marcado BYD para sus propias pruebas, lo que confirma que la carrera por esta tecnología, a veces considerada el "Santo Grial" de las baterías, está más intensa que nunca.
Promesas. Las baterías de estado sólido prometen resolver de un plumazo varios de los grandes problemas del coche eléctrico actual, entre ellos más autonomía con menos peso, cargas más rápidas y un riesgo mucho menor de incendio, al sustituir el electrolito líquido por uno sólido.
Que los dos gigantes chinos del sector, que además compiten entre sí, se hayan planteado como fecha de sus respectivas pruebas 2027 marca un punto de inflexión. Sin embargo, eso no significa que el año que viene veamos ya coches en concesionarios con baterías de estado sólido, ya que para eso aún queda un buen rato.
En detalle. Según recoge el portal especializado libattery.net, CATL respondía a algunas de las preguntas de los inversores asegurando que su desarrollo en baterías de estado sólido es "líder en la industria" y que la compañía prevé iniciar líneas piloto de producción a pequeña escala en 2027. Es la primera vez que la firma pone una fecha concreta sobre la mesa, y lo hace apenas unos días antes de que BYD recibiera seis nuevas patentes relacionadas con esta misma tecnología, según cuentan desde CarNewsChina.
La respuesta de BYD. Las patentes de BYD giran en torno al objetivo de mantener un contacto fiable entre los materiales sólidos del cátodo y el electrolito a lo largo de miles de ciclos de carga y descarga, uno de los grandes quebraderos de cabeza de esta tecnología. Su apuesta es un cátodo de doble electrolito que combina partículas de haluro, más estables, con partículas de sulfuro, mejores conduciendo iones de litio.
Cuatro de las patentes se centran en la química de los materiales (desde capas intermedias que evitan reacciones no deseadas hasta cátodos de doble capa que combinan materiales monocristalinos y policristalinos) mientras que las otras dos se centran en la fabricación, incluyendo un criterio de control de calidad que exige que al menos el 60% del perímetro de cada partícula de cátodo esté en contacto con el electrolito. BYD también ha señalado 2027 como el año en el que empezará a fabricar estas celdas a pequeña escala, con pruebas en prototipos camuflados.
Entre líneas. Que ambas compañías fijen la misma fecha no significa que las baterías de estado sólido vayan a llegar mañana al mercado de masas. El propio presidente de CATL, Robin Zeng, reconocía en junio que su adopción comercial "todavía tardará años" y admitió que las celdas de la firma se encuentran solo en el nivel 4 de 9 en la escala TRL (Technology Readiness Level), que mide la madurez de una tecnología.
El objetivo de CATL para 2027 es alcanzar los niveles 7 u 8, según explicó su científico jefe, Wu Kai, algo que permitiría iniciar la producción piloto y las primeras validaciones reales, pero que sigue quedando lejos de una fabricación en volumen. De hecho, CATL sitúa el umbral de la producción a gran escala en un millón de vehículos al año, una cifra que no espera alcanzar antes de 2030.
Quién podrá comprarlas primero. Según ha explicado la propia CATL, las limitaciones técnicas y de fabricación harán que los primeros lotes comerciales de baterías de estado sólido se reserven para modelos premium, con precios a partir de 250.000 yuanes (unos 37.000 dólares). Es decir, que aunque la tecnología empiece a probarse en 2027, tardará bastante más en llegar a los coches eléctricos de gama media y de acceso.
Además, CATL y BYD no están solas. Y es que fabricantes como Dongfeng o Changan, y empresas emergentes como Pure Lithium, también han entrado en la carrera, sabiendo que se trata de una tecnología que de golpe y porrazo podría reordenar el actual mapa de las empresas más importantes.

articles.title: IPTV, Streaming illégal : une solution radicale est proposée à l'Union européenne pour tout couper en 30 minutes
articles.text:
Les « recommandations incitatives » ne fonctionnent plus. C’est en substance ce qu’explique une étude menée pour le Parlement européen par le professeur Giovanni Maria Riccio. Le constat est que la stratégie adoptée en 2023 basée sur la bonne volonté ne suffit pas. Le piratage en direct d’un flux IPTV et le streaming illégal du sport vont trop vite et la riposte européenne est trop désordonnée. Le rapport propose donc de passer aux choses sérieuses avec une vraie loi européenne contraignante.
30 minutes chrono pour bloquer un flux illégal
Le plan s’inspire du système italien « Piracy Shield » qui impose un blocage en 30 minutes maximum dès qu’un flux illégal est repéré. La grosse différence, c’est que cette obligation ne toucherait pas seulement les opérateurs télécoms. Les serveurs DNS de géants comme Google, les réseaux de diffusion de contenu comme Cloudflare, les hébergeurs et même les services de VPN devraient couper les accès. Pour gérer tout ça, chaque pays membre devrait créer sa propre police du web, sur le modèle de l’autorité italienne AGCOM.
Des tribunaux ont déjà commencé à ordonner des blocages similaires, comme à Paris où des VPN et des DNS ont été visés. Le problème, c’est que bloquer une adresse IP ou un nom de domaine reste une méthode plutôt musclée. Cela coupe les pirates, mais aussi parfois des sites parfaitement légitimes au passage. En Espagne, des blocages demandés par LaLiga ont ainsi rendu inaccessibles plus de 554 000 domaines, rendant temporairement inaccessibles les sites d’UNICEF, d’Amnesty International ou encore des services d’Amazon.
Des règles pour limiter la casse et une baisse des prix nécessaire
Pour éviter de fermer des sites à la pelle à chaque coup de sifflet, le rapport propose plusieurs garde-fous. Les blocages devraient impérativement s’arrêter dès la fin du match. L’étude cite aussi des chercheurs qui demandent d’interdire le blocage par IP et de faire payer aux ayants droit les dégâts causés quand un site légitime est coupé par erreur.
Découvrez : 12 sites gratuits pour regarder des films et séries en streaming (légalement)
Mais le rapport pointe surtout le vrai fond du problème : regarder du sport coûte beaucoup trop cher. La dispersion des droits TV oblige les fans à cumuler des abonnements hors de prix, quand ils ne sont pas bloqués par des restrictions géographiques. Bloquer les sites ne suffira jamais si les chaînes ne proposent pas des offres plus simples et plus abordables. Pour l’instant, toutes ces propositions restent de simples recommandations sur la table de la Commission européenne.

articles.title: How Tata Trusts and Sridhar Vembu kept the first MRI scanner built in India out of a multinational’s hands
articles.text:
How Tata Trusts and Sridhar Vembu kept the first MRI scanner built in India out of a multinational’s hands
The Bengaluru-based company builds a full-body 1.5-tesla MRI scanner engineered and manufactured in India, designed to run without liquid helium, with its first clinical installation at a cancer centre near Nagpur.
India has built most major categories of hospital equipment domestically; the MRI scanner has been a rare exception. The magnets, the electronics and the software have come from a small number of multinational manufacturers, and Indian hospitals have paid import prices for them.
The running cost matters as much as the purchase price. Conventional scanners are cooled by liquid helium, which is scarce, expensive and difficult to transport, and the machines are heavy enough that hospitals often can't install them just anywhere in a building. Innovations was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Arjun Arunachalam, who holds MS and PhD degrees from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and worked at the GE Global Research Center in New York between 2006 and 2008. He left GE in October 2008 intending to start a company.
A year of fundraising came to nothing, and Arunachalam joined IIT Bombay as a faculty member in electrical engineering. A grant from Spring Singapore, received after his family relocated in 2013, paid for a small test scanner.
In May 2016, he approached Tata Trusts with a proposal to build MRI scanners in India. The Trusts introduced him to the Foundation for Innovation and Social Entrepreneurship (FISE), where the core team was employed in the early years. A prototype installed at the Sathya Sai Institute of Higher Medical Sciences in Bengaluru produced its first images in March 2018.
A magnet that does not need helium
The product is a compact, full-body 1.5 tesla scanner, the clinical standard field strength. The company says it is designed to run in both fixed and mobile configurations, and to hold image quality under difficult installation conditions.
The design choice that carries the rest is the magnet. Voxelgrids uses a superconducting magnet that does not rely on liquid helium, which the company says takes roughly 40%off the cost of building a scanner. Coverage of the December 2025 deployment put the machine at two to three tonnes, against about six tonnes for a conventional system.
Weight determines where a scanner can go. A lighter machine can fit on an upper floor, in a smaller hospital, or on a mobile platform, which is why the company is targeting smaller cities and towns. Voxelgrids says its electronics are packaged tightly around the magnet, which it credits with lower power draw.
The engineering was done in-house, covering software, electronics and the cryogenic magnet. Arunachalam holds a US patent, filed in December 2015 and assigned to the company, covering part of the scanner's design. Voxelgrids was certified to ISO 13485 in mid-2020 and received its commercial manufacturing and sales licence in June 2023.
One installation, and a commercial launch still ahead
Voxelgrids' first clinical installation went in at the Chandrapur Cancer Care Foundation near Nagpur, unveiled in December 2025 and now used for patient diagnostics. Tata Trusts, which backed the company through development, also supported it by placing an order for a machine.
Zoho Corporation led a $5 million Series A round in 2021, which Arunachalam has said gave the company enough runway to keep developing the scanner. According to Business Today, Tata Trusts, and later Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu, were instrumental in keeping the company afloat during that period. Under the National Biopharma Mission, the Department of Biotechnology contributed Rs 12 crores of the Rs 17 crores spent developing the scanner, routed through the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC).
The Bengaluru facility is set up for 20 to 25 scanners a year. Arunachalam said in December 2025 that a full commercial launch was expected by the end of the financial year, and that the company would raise a larger round as it approached volume production. The team stands at 33 members today.
Beyond the Chandrapur installation and the Tata Trusts order, no customer, contract value or revenue figure has been disclosed, and the commercial launch Arunachalam pointed to has not been separately announced since.
(This story has been researched and compiled using publicly available information.)

articles.title: Souveraineté numérique : trouvez des alternatives et améliorez votre score avec cette application open source
articles.text:
Souveraineté numérique : trouvez des alternatives et améliorez votre score avec cette application open source
Curieux de savoir dans quelle mesure vous utilisez des applications open source sur votre smartphone ? Voici LibreFind, également conçue pour vous aider à trouver des alternatives aux applications propriétaires.
La course à la dégooglisation n'est pas un sprint, mais un marathon. Changer la plupart de ses applications propriétaires, émanant souvent des GAFAM, par des alternatives open source, peut s'avérer complexe. Sans même évoquer la difficulté pour remplacer des habitudes souvent bien ancrées (J’ai essayé de remplacer Google Maps pendant 4 ans : mon bilan sans concession), la première étape, à savoir trouver une solution alternative, peut s'avérer fastidieuse. Heureusement, de nombreuses solutions façon AlternativeTo existent, à l'image de celle du jour : LibreFind.
Une ressource pour passer à l'open source
Le fonctionnement de LibreFind est simple. Une fois installée, l'application Android scanne les logiciels installés sur le terminal et commence par donner un score de souveraineté. Celui-ci représente "dans quelle mesure votre vie numérique est alimentée par les logiciels libres et open source". Malgré ma volonté ces dernières années de remplacer la plupart de mes applications propriétaires, je n'ai obtenu qu'un famélique 9 %.
Il faut dire que mes 24 applis libres sont noyées dans 222 applications et services propriétaires. Normal après tout, puisque même sans les utiliser, les logiciels des GAFAM et les nombreux services d'Android restent présents sur mon appareil (rarement par choix), et que bien des logiciels (banque, administratif, streaming...) ne disposent tout simplement pas d'alternatives. Ce système de score est donc surtout indicatif et permet de se rendre compte de l'ampleur de la tâche pour réduire l'emprise de Google et consorts sans embrasser un OS alternatif.
Mais là où LibreFind se montre réellement utile, c'est dans sa fonctionnalité de recherche pour découvrir des alternatives open source à ses logiciels propriétaires. La solution n'est cependant pas parfaite. La forme est un brin brute de décoffrage et le fond a parfois quelques ratés. Des alternatives pourtant bien réelles ne sont pas toujours listées quand elles le devraient, et les solutions suggérées sont parfois un peu trop rares. Couplée à d'autres solutions, LibreFind peut malgré tout faire office de bon point de départ pour effectuer sa transition open source.
Côté disponibilité, LibreFind n'est sans surprise pas disponible sur le PlayStore. Il faudra se tourner au choix vers GitHub ou encore F-Droid. Relevons cependant que l'application risque bientôt de disparaitre partiellement. En effet, en réponse à la décision de Google de demander prochainement l'identité de tous les développeurs proposant une application sur un terminal Android certifié, le développeur de LibreFind préfèrera retirer son application de ces derniers le moment venu.

articles.title: Microsoft Publisher : il vous reste 2 mois pour trouver une alternative
articles.text:
Microsoft a envoyé un email à ses abonnés Microsoft 365 pour justifier l'arrêt de Publisher, prévu le 1er octobre 2026. L'éditeur y explique avoir observé un usage limité du logiciel et préfère concentrer ses ressources sur des outils comme Copilot.
Il est temps de sauvegarder vos documents
Dans un email intitulé "Important update to your Microsoft 365 subscription", repéré par Windows Latest, Microsoft indique que Publisher fait partie des outils les moins sollicités et justifie ainsi sa disparition par la volonté de mieux investir dans les usages réels de ses clients, notamment Microsoft 365 Copilot.
Les abonnés à Microsoft 365, qui paient un accès mensuel ou annuel à la suite bureautique, perdront tout accès à Publisher à partir du 1er octobre 2026. Le logiciel ne s'ouvrira plus, quel que soit le fichier concerné. Pour les détenteurs d'une licence perpétuelle, achetée une seule fois via Office 2021 LTSC, pourront continuer à utiliser Publisher un peu plus longtemps, jusqu'à la fin du support de cette version le 13 octobre 2026. Passé cette date, le logiciel restera installé sur l'ordinateur mais ne recevra plus aucune mise à jour de sécurité.
Pour éviter de perdre l'accès à ses documents, Microsoft recommande de convertir chaque fichier Publisher en PDF ou en document Word avant l'échéance. La manipulation s'effectue fichier par fichier, sans outil de conversion groupée. Il faut donc ouvrir le document, passer par le menu Fichier, Enregistrer sous, puis sélectionner le format PDF. Cette étape concerne en priorité les abonnés Microsoft 365 : passé cette échéance, ils ne pourront plus ouvrir ni modifier leurs fichiers Publisher. Ceux qui cherchent à conserver des fonctionnalités de mise en page proches de celles de Publisher peuvent aussi se tourner vers des solutions installées localement, en dehors de l'écosystème Microsoft, plutôt que vers les seules alternatives intégrées à Microsoft 365.
Et ensuite ? Quoi ?
En annonçant la fin de Publisher en mars 2025, Microsoft avait publié un tableau de concordances de fonctionnalités :
- Annonces ou flyers : Word, PowerPoint ou Designer.
- Brochures : Word ou PowerPoint
- Bannières, panneaux, affiches : PowerPoint ou Designer.
- Certificats : Word ou PowerPoint.
- Cartes de visite : Word ou PowerPoint
- Factures, applications et formulaires professionnels : Word.
- Calendriers : Word ou PowerPoint.
- Enveloppes : Word.
- Étiquettes : Word.
- En-tête : Word.
- Bulletin : Word.
- Programmes, projets de papier plié : Word.
- Cartes (Salutation, Compliment, etc.) : Word, PowerPoint ou Designer.
À noter que LibreOffice Draw intègre une bibliothèque dédiée, libmspub, capable de décoder la quasi-totalité des fichiers Publisher pour les convertir en éléments vectoriels et calques modifiables. En pratique, le résultat reste fidèle sur les mises en page simples, mais peut se dégrader sur des documents plus complexes. En tout cas, ça ne coûte rien de tester, c'est gratuit et open source.

articles.title: Renault augmente l'autonomie de la R5 électrique grâce à des optimisations matérielles
articles.text:
Alors que la Renault 5 E-Tech enchaîne les succès commerciaux sur le marché français, un argument de plus penche en sa faveur au moment d’acheter une voiture électrique. Sur le configurateur du constructeur, les autonomies mixtes WLTP annoncées sont en hausse sur plusieurs déclinaisons : jusqu’à une vingtaine de kilomètres en plus.
D’abord repérée par nos confrères d’Automobile Propre ce 10 août 2026, cette petite mise à jour technique nous a été officiellement confirmée par Renault.
Des consommations en baisse pour la R5
Même si elle est loin d’être spécialement gourmande, la Renault 5 disposait d’une marge de progression pour faire baisser ses consommations. L’augmentation des autonomies constatée le 10 août témoigne qu’il est possible de gagner quelques précieux kilomètres en plus.
La version équipée de la batterie de 52 kWh affiche désormais jusqu’à 431 km WLTP (sur la finition Evolution), contre 416 km lors du lancement. Même constat pour la « petite » batterie de 40 kWh (moteur 120 ch), qui passe de 312 à 321 km WLTP.
Les nouvelles autonomies selon les versions :
| Version | Autonomie (WLTP) | Consommation (WLTP) | 
|---|---|---|
| 120 ch autonomie urbaine – Evolution | 321 km | 14,2 kWh/100 km | 
| 120 ch autonomie urbaine – Techno | 317 km | 14,4 kWh/100 km | 
| 150 ch autonomie confort – Evolution | 431 km | 13,9 kWh/100 km | 
| 150 ch autonomie confort – Techno | 425 km | 14,1 kWh/100 km | 
| 150 ch autonomie confort – Iconic cinq | 422 km | 14,2 kWh/100 km | 
| 150 ch autonomie confort – Roland-Garros | 424 km | 14,2 kWh/100 km | 
Les améliorations en matière de consommation sont légères, mais elles suffisent à modifier le résultat à l’homologation. Est-ce que cela changera radicalement le quotidien des conducteurs ? Pas vraiment, mais le plaisir de la R5 réside dans ses qualités d’ensemble, notamment en matière de tenue de route.
Selon des rumeurs, Renault préparerait par ailleurs d’autres évolutions qui devraient permettre d’améliorer davantage l’autonomie de la R5.
Des optimisations matérielles, mais pas de détails apportés
Comment Renault a-t-il réussi à gratter ces précieux kilomètres sans toucher à la taille des batteries ? Selon toute vraisemblance, il ne s’agit pas d’un simple réétalonnage logiciel que l’on pourrait recevoir « over-the-air » (OTA) sans passer par l’atelier. C’est ce que Tesla avait déjà réussi à faire avec ses modèles, mais ce n’est pas le cas pour la Renault 5.
Renault nous a bien confirmé « qu’ils ont réalisé différentes optimisations, qui se traduisent par des gains sur les consommations » sans apporter davantage de détails techniques. Mais comme la marque précise que l’ouverture des commandes a été anticipée, cela confirme qu’il s’agit bien d’une variante sensiblement différente du modèle initial, et pas seulement au niveau logiciel.
Ces quelques kilomètres supplémentaires sont donc réservés aux nouvelles commandes enregistrées. Les propriétaires de la première heure pourront se rassurer en se disant que leurs 416 km théoriques (ou les 310 km WLTP de la version à autonomie urbaine) restent largement suffisants au quotidien.
Une mise à jour de l’entrée de gamme « Five »
Nos confrères d’Automobile Propre ont également levé un autre lièvre : ils ont remarqué que le modèle d’entrée de gamme « Five » affichait des données modifiées en Belgique. Le modèle n’est plus indiqué comme faisant 95 ch, mais 110 ch. La taille de la batterie serait également différente : 37 kWh au lieu de 40 kWh pour 315 km d’autonomie. Sur le papier, cette modification de capacité semble étonnante (liée à la façon dont sont composés les modules de cellules NMC), à moins que la batterie ne soit passée sur une autre chimie de type LFP.
De l’autre côté de la frontière, la version Five est également présentée sur sa fiche technique avec un chargeur AC de 7 kW et une charge rapide DC de 80 kW de série. Et ce changement serait une petite révolution si cela se confirmait également pour la France. Au moment de publier cet article, la fiche technique de la R5 Five n’a pas été changée sur le configurateur français.

articles.title: Sicherheitsexperte erklärt, warum Hacker bei Google einen Vor- und Nachnamen haben
articles.text:
Cyberkriminalität: Warum Hackergruppen bei Google jetzt einen Vor- und Nachnamen haben
Von Anonymous über Sandworm bis hin zu Fancy Bear: Seit Jahren vergibt die Cybersicherheitsbranche Namen an Hackergruppen. Trotzdem kann es manchmal schwerfallen, bestimmte Akteur:innen klar zuzuordnen. Der Grund: Nicht alle Unternehmen benennen die Gruppen einheitlich. Google hat sein Benennungssystem im vergangenen Monat überarbeitet. Shane Huntley, der als Chief Technology Officer bei der Google Threat Intelligence Group tätig ist, gibt einen Einblick, wie genau das neue System funktioniert.
Hackerangriffe nehmen weltweit spürbar zu
Auch die deutsche Wirtschaft gerät zunehmend ins Visier krimineller Hackergruppen. Im vergangenen Jahr berichteten im Rahmen einer Bitkom-Umfrage 87 Prozent der Unternehmen von Datendiebstahl, Industriespionage oder Sabotage – ein Jahr zuvor lag der Anteil noch bei 81 Prozent. Vor allem der Anteil an Angriffen, die sich nach Russland und China zurückverfolgen lassen, hat zugenommen: 46 Prozent der betroffenen Unternehmen stellten mindestens einen Angriff aus Russland fest, ebenso viele aus China. Weitere 28 Prozent konnten mindestens einen Angriff einem ausländischen Nachrichtendienst zuordnen. Laut Bitkom lag dieser Anteil im Vorjahr noch bei 20 Prozent und 2023 sogar nur bei sieben Prozent.
Das US-amerikanische Cybersicherheitsunternehmen Mandiant war das erste, das ein Benennungsschema für Hackergruppen einführte. Lange Zeit kam dabei das Kürzel APT in Verbindung mit einer beliebigen Zahl zum Einsatz. Inzwischen ist das Unternehmen Teil von Google. Um das System zu vereinfachen, wurde ein neues Schema eingeführt. Der Name einer Hackergruppe setzt sich jetzt aus zwei Wörtern zusammen: Der „Vorname“ ist ein einprägsames, zufällig gewähltes Wort, das zweite gibt einen Hinweis auf das Herkunftsland. „Castle” steht für China, „Ion” für den Iran, „Neptune” für Nordkorea und „Relic” für Russland. Wie Huntley gegenüber Techcrunch erklärte, war diese Umstellung notwendig, um sowohl intern als auch extern mehr Klarheit zu schaffen.
Codenamen sollen bessere Übersicht bieten
Das Ziel der eindeutigen Benennung bestehe darin, ein grundlegendes Verständnis dafür zu erlangen, wer wen angreift und wie diese Angriffe erfolgen. So könnten Organisationen Bedrohungen schneller erkennen, sich vorbereiten und sie im Idealfall abwehren oder Vorfälle zügiger untersuchen. All das sei laut Huntley nur möglich, wenn man die Hackergruppen namentlich benennt und konsequent verfolgt. „Wenn man tatsächlich von ihnen gehackt wird oder mit einem Vorfall konfrontiert ist, sind all diese Details – wie sich diese Akteur:innen verhalten, was sie tun und was sie in der Vergangenheit getan haben – von entscheidender Bedeutung, um angemessen reagieren zu können und auch den eigenen Schutz gegen diese Bedrohungen zu optimieren“, so Huntley.
Die Verfolgung staatlich geförderter Hacker sei zwar eine Herausforderung, aber einfacher als die Verfolgung von Cyberkriminellen und Hacker-for-Hire-Gruppen. Staatliche Hacker verfolgten meist konsistentere Ziele und Aktivitäten, während sich die Mitglieder krimineller Gruppen öfter ändern könnten. Aber warum verwenden nicht einfach alle Unternehmen dieselben Codenamen? Laut Huntley gibt es dafür einen einfachen Grund: Jedes Unternehmen habe aufgrund seiner eigenen Daten eine etwas andere Sicht auf jede Gruppe. „Niemand hat einen perfekten Überblick“, so der Experte gegenüber Techcrunch. „Wir entwickeln unser Modell und unser bestmögliches Verständnis, aber wir werden nie alles darüber wissen, was vor sich geht.“

articles.title: Microsoft admite que no copiará el Liquid Glass del iPhone en Windows 11 y tiene una buena razón
articles.text:
Cuando Apple anunció iOS 26 con Liquid Glass, muchos usuarios pensaron que se trataba de una idea original nunca antes vista. La realidad es que Microsoft hizo algo parecido hace casi dos décadas con Windows Vista y Aero, una interfaz parecida que muchos todavía recuerdan con cariño. Con la moda impuesta por Apple, muchos se preguntan si Windows 11 adoptará este esquema y ofrecerá un diseño cristalino, una decisión que sus creadores no piensan aplicar.
De acuerdo con WindowsLatest, Microsoft acaba de cerrar la puerta a una de las peticiones más repetidas por su comunidad de usuarios. El gigante tecnológico dijo que no habrá control nativo de transparencia en Windows 11, por lo que la única alternativa serán los desarrolladores externos. March Rogers, director de diseño en Microsoft, explicó que un cambio visual tipo Liquid Glass a gran escala requiere un análisis exhaustivo.
El jefe del Departamento de Diseño respondió directamente a las preguntas de varios usuarios que pedían un deslizador similar al de iOS 26. Rogers dejó claro que además del análisis, se debe valorar el impacto en usabilidad y accesibilidad. El directivo añadió que Windows 11 no permite aumentar la transparencia por encima de los valores predeterminados, ya que eso podría afectar la legibilidad del sistema operativo.
Un usuario respondió a Rogers con una captura de pantalla de su escritorio, el cual personalizó usando Windhawk. Si este nombre no te suena, se trata de una herramienta de terceros que permite modificar la interfaz de Windows 11. El jefe de diseño terminó reconociendo que Microsoft observa lo que ya ofrece su comunidad de desarrolladores antes de decidir si vale la pena construir algo similar de forma nativa.
Windows 11 no tendrá una interfaz Liquid Glass nativa
March Rogers mencionó directamente el trabajo de proyectos como Windhawk, que aportan su granito de arena a la personalización. La conclusión es que no habrá cambios inmediatos en las opciones de transparencia de Windows, al menos en el corto plazo. Si esperabas un Liquid Glass, la única opción será optar por herramientas de terceros, aunque algunas podrían generar inestabilidad.
Lo curioso de toda la conversación es que Windows ya experimentó con una estética similar a la de Apple hace casi veinte años. Aero Glass, la interfaz que debutó con Windows Vista en 2007, ofrecía un aspecto esmerilado y transparente en ventanas y menús mucho antes de que Apple popularizara este lenguaje visual. Lamentablemente, Microsoft abandonó ese camino con Windows 8, cuando apostó por el diseño plano que después evolucionó hacia Acrylic y Mica.
El regreso de esta estética con Liquid Glass y otros sistemas que le han copiado le dio esperanza a miles de usuarios que pedían de vuelta la interfaz Aero en Windows 11. Uno de los que mantuvo la conversación con Rogers afirmó que una función nativa del sistema operativo siempre ofrece más estabilidad y menos riesgo de errores.
Si bien el usuario tiene razón, lo cierto es que Microsoft no está dispuesta a apostar por un diseño que podría romper más elementos del sistema operativo. En una entrevista con Windows Central, el jefe de Diseño e Investigación para Windows y Dispositivos, Marcus Ash, admitió que Microsoft no ha modernizado Windows 11 al ritmo que los usuarios esperan.
Ash dijo que modernizar las viejas interfaces no consiste simplemente en rediseñar la pantalla. Los ingenieros de Microsoft tienen que construir en paralelo las herramientas y frameworks que puedan sostener la interfaz sin perder las capacidades, rendimiento o funciones que ya existían.

articles.title: GeForce Now exploit unlocks full Windows desktop access
articles.text:
In brief: GeForce Now is a cloud gaming service that lets users stream games over the internet in limited sessions. As a pair of modders recently discovered, however, a bit of tinkering can turn it into a formidable system for offloading demanding computing tasks.
GeForce Now can apparently do much more than simply stream a selection of supported games using the AV1 codec. Two modders known as "Zortos" and "dpadGuy" have discovered a "trick" to gain full desktop access to the streaming service, allowing them to run custom games and software directly on Nvidia's hardware.
The modders explained how they achieved this unprecedented result in a video tutorial. The clip essentially provides a step-by-step guide on how to access the remote desktop, although they warn that the method only works with a paid GeForce Now subscription. Free-tier users and GeForce Now Alliance Partner services remain limited to AV1 game streaming.
The tutorial is based on the free-to-play game Trove and GeForce Now's ability to expose the Steam client's full interface. From within the current Steam session, users need to access the client's browser and locate a specific executable file in Trove's installation folder. They then need to replace the file with a special version provided by the modders and launch it to finally access the remote desktop.
GeForce Now machines can provide some hefty hardware specifications. Zortos said he was able to access an "Ultimate"-tier machine equipped with an AMD Epyc 9375F 32-core CPU and a GeForce RTX 5080 GPU. The system has 48GB of VRAM and 56GB of total system RAM.
 – Zortos (@Zortosdev) August 7, 2026
The tutorial demonstrates how the newly discovered desktop access could be used to install Wallpaper Engine from Steam or customize the Windows taskbar. More generally, it could provide broader access to Nvidia's hardware resources, raising significant security and trust concerns. Later, Zortos used the powerful remote machines to install custom AI models, promising that more "juicy" demonstrations are on the way.
In any case, the Trove-based method for breaking into Nvidia's cloud gaming service does not appear to be foolproof. Some users who tried the same trick experienced a few unexpected issues, including Windows sessions closing automatically or being unable to download the custom executable file to Trove's folder. Some said the Trove method no longer works, although Zortos reiterated that this is not the case.

articles.title: Intel is Selling $15B of its Own Stock to Build More Fab Capacity
articles.text:
Monday, August 10th 2026
	
		
	
	
	
Intel is Selling $15B of its Own Stock to Build More Fab Capacity
Intel announced today that it will officially offer a $15 billion underwritten public offering of common stock to fund its capital-intensive foundry expansion. This move means the company is looking to dilute existing share ownership by issuing more shares to raise additional capital through its public offering. Supporting this deal is an elite group of investment banks, including JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and Citigroup, who are acting as joint book-running managers. Intel operates in one of the most capital-intensive industries, where maintaining leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing requires tens of billions of US dollars. Therefore, the company needs additional funds without taking on loans or requiring external investors. Underwriters have a 30-day option to purchase an additional $2.25 billion worth of shares at the public share price, pushing the grand total to $17.25 billion
Regarding the main question of why Intel is doing this, the company noted that "Customers continue to signal a strong and sustainable demand environment, driven by unprecedented investment in AI compute. Progress in emerging areas, including physical AI, purpose-built silicon, advanced packaging, and external wafers, represents significant growth opportunities for Intel." This indicates that Intel's external customers are eager to use Intel Foundry services, including silicon manufacturing and advanced packaging, in quantities that exceed Intel's current capacity.When Intel's CEO Lip-Bu Tan took the helm, he stated that the company would only invest significant financial resources into manufacturing capacity if there were sufficient customer demand. Since Intel is raising significant funds for expansion, it suggests that customer demand is here. While major shareholders are facing dilution at this point, the goal of this new stock offering is to fund the company's expansion so it remains relevant in the advanced packaging and leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing race, without relying on external financing.

articles.title: A researcher bought noreply.net. Companies started sending him secrets.
articles.text:
Cory Solovewicz receives more unwanted emails than you. Seriously—it’s a lot more. Since December 2024, one of the domains at which the security researcher receives email has registered 401,796 messages—by his calculations that’s an average of 699.99 pings per day.
This deluge isn’t the regular flood of spam, newsletters, and unwanted deals that fill many people’s inboxes. Instead, companies and other organizations are inadvertently sending Solovewicz other people’s private information and company secrets. Over the last few years, he’s received injury reports from a city government, confirmation of people’s pizza orders, and account setup emails from a school platform. “I get service orders for people that need repairs. I get lots of test platform credentials,” says Solovewicz, a security researcher and consultant.
Solovewicz is receiving the avalanche of messages as he’s the owner of the domains noreply.us and noreply.net, which he purchased in 2020 and 2024, respectively. After originally planning to use the noreply.us domain as a catch-all email—which receives mail sent to any @ address on that domain—to filter messages and enhance his privacy, the researcher quickly noticed that other systems were sending mail to @noreply.us addresses. “I created an accidental honeypot,” Solovewicz tells WIRED. “I had no idea it was going to turn into this.”
Companies may send emails to [companyname]@noreply.net or similar variations believing they aren’t going anywhere, or could not be monitored in any way. Broadly it’s also possible that they may transform a person’s individual email address to send to one of these placeholder style domains if someone leaves a company or deletes their account.
What started out as a personal email project has become a large-scale effort to warn businesses and other groups that they have misconfigured their internal systems and are accidentally sharing sensitive information. Solovewicz, who presented his work at the Defcon security conference yesterday, says ultimately he is relieved that he ended up with the domains rather than criminal hackers or nation states who could use the data maliciously.

articles.title: Why tech vendors are key to solving AI's adoption problem
articles.text:
Why tech vendors are key to solving AI's adoption problem
Companies will succeed with AI adoption by hiring technology vendors
Many companies successfully complete AI pilots, but a lot struggle to scale AI application across their organizations. Only 15% of AI initiatives ever manage to truly scale.
Research from Boston Consulting Group suggests that only 26% of companies have developed the capabilities needed to move beyond pilots and generate meaningful value from AI tools. Meanwhile, McKinsey estimates that while almost every organization is experimenting with generative AI, only a small minority are seeing material financial impact across the business.
Founder and CEO of AI-native platform Ravical.
The technology is not the bottleneck.
Large language models offer a powerful solution that supports employees in various tasks, such as research, content generation, document analysis, meeting summary or task management. Despite these advances, teams still battle to turn AI capability into measurable business outcomes.
It is a translation problem.
There is a lack of depth that prevents these tools from meeting the needs of a specific industry and organization. General models are good at understanding language and information. But they have a hard time connecting them to workflows, regulations, governance requirements and operational nuances that rule industries, such as accounting, legal service, healthcare or manufacturing.
There needs to be an expert to bridge the gap between the capabilities of AI and the requirements of a profession.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
1. A new role at the intersection of the technology and an industry
Technology vendors have traditionally been measured by the quality of their products. This is no longer enough.
Today, their role goes far beyond delivering a functional platform. They now actively contribute to the digital transformation of an organization. This includes sharing best practices, providing ongoing technical support, designing workflows, optimizing for governance and long-term application. All to support smooth product deployment.
Different industries are moving towards this same idea from different angles. When there is an intermediary that focuses on customer success, it translates capability into outcomes. Early examples of this are the rise of new jobs such as Customer Value Managers and Forward Deployed Engineers. These are professionals whose primary objective is ensuring the technology generates value for employees and the business overall.
Every industry is beginning to create its own version of the role.
In accounting, we see the emergence of so-called 'Accountancy Engineers'. They are trained accountants with deep accounting expertise and technical capability. Rather than working from a specification document, they sit next to a firm's team and co-design the workflow with them, building the automation alongside the people who will actually use it.
They build workflows tailored to how the profession works, effectively automating repetitive tasks and processes that answer to the challenges of accountancy. Just as important, they train the firm's own accountants to become the practice's internal AI architects, so the capability stays inside the firm long after the initial rollout.
For instance, they work to connect backend accounting systems with operational tools and cloud infrastructure and ensure that automated financial processes align with regulatory reporting and data governance requirements. This avoids generic automation bolted onto old corporate systems, resulting in a tailored integration.
And every pattern they uncover in the field, a workaround, a recurring bottleneck, a workflow nobody had written down, feeds straight back into the vendor's own product roadmap, the same feedback loop that made Forward Deployed Engineers indispensable at Palantir.
AI adoption rarely fails because the model is not capable enough. It does not go through because employees don't know where the technology fits within their daily work.
2. Supported human integration for smoother AI adoption
General AI models are horizontal by design. They struggle to generate specific materials and in-depth data analysis tailored to a single industry, since they were built to serve every industry at once.
Firms that engage with vendor partners see successful integration because they receive industry-specific guidance and training that empowers staff to firmly handle AI tools.
In general, people are hesitant when encountering new tools and processes. Leaders worry about governance, security and regulatory compliance. Employees wonder whether they can trust AI-generated outputs.
On the individual level, teams experiment with consumer AI tools, creating fragmented workflows and introducing the growing problem of "shadow AI", where employees expose sensitive company information through personal AI accounts.
Without governance, training and clear operational guidance, organizations risk creating thousands of disconnected AI users rather than a coordinated AI strategy.
Technology vendors make a difference by collaborating with product managers, financial controllers, and cross-functional engineering teams.
Together, they design an integrated system architecture that includes existing technology, develop governance frameworks that reduce risk, and create education programs and processes that support positive engagement across a company. This ultimately generates trust and safety, ensuring a successful adoption.
Vendors provide the missing layer between technological possibility and organizational reality.
3. From one-off projects to long-term implementation
AI adoption does not have a finish line.
The technology almost changes every week. New models emerge. Capabilities improve. Costs change. Workflows that were impossible six months ago become routine today. That means AI cannot be treated like a traditional ERP rollout or cloud migration.
Technology vendors are uniquely positioned to provide continuous support. They know the ins and outs of the product and understand the challenges faced by organizations, which means they can tailor the approach to find the right solutions. Plus, they monitor the rapid pace of AI innovation while understanding how those advances affect specific industries.
Instead of trying to interpret an increasingly complex AI landscape themselves, teams can rely on vendors to get a clear picture of technical breakthroughs and how they can be relevant to the business and employees.
4. Sell business outcomes, not a model
The vendors who only sell AI models are selling half the answer. AI adoption fails when teams are left to figure out the product on their own, with no one in the room translating the platform into the firm's own workflow.
Every organization will eventually have access to powerful models. What will differentiate them is their ability to combine AI expertise with industry expertise.
Technology vendors who succeed will be the ones who live between the technology and the profession, translating AI capability into trusted, scalable business outcomes. Accountancy Engineers, and every version of that role now emerging across other industries, is what that translation looks like in practice.

articles.title: Roku now has a 24/7 AI slop channel
articles.text:
Roku is a pretty good platform.
With its robust offering of channels, including those with free ad-supported streaming TV (FAST) programming, it’s a nice option to have in this oversaturated and increasingly expensive streaming market. But enshittification comes for us all, and Roku is sadly no exception.
Last week, Cord Cutters News spotted that Roku quietly added a new channel called Fairground AI. As the name suggests, it features AI-generated content. And because it’s free, it runs ads, which are also AI-generated. (“Yo dawg, we heard you like AI slop, so we put AI slop inside of your AI slop.”)
Per Variety, Fairground AI hails from Colin Petrie-Norris, the founder of the streaming service Xumo. The company says it offers the world’s first-ever FAST channel “devoted to AI cinema” that features content from “over 100 of the best AI filmmakers from around the world.” Of course, that is a hilarious thing to boast about, especially since there is no such thing as an AI “filmmaker” in any true sense of the word.
But hey, Elon Musk and his fellow AI-pilled losers can get excited about all of the “films” that Fairground AI will feature.
Via: Futurism
