articles.title: Oslo-based Visoid raises €2.2 million to scale its AI visualisation platform for architects | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Visoid, an Oslo-based AI visualisation platform for architects and industry professionals, has secured €2.16 million ($2.5 million) in fresh funding to support the company’s next stage of growth.
The round was led by Skyfall Ventures, with participation from existing investors StartupLab, OBOS and Antler, alongside new investors Farvatn and byFounders Angel Collective.
“Architects have been using the same software for the past 30 years, and they were reluctant to try new ones. It’s amazing to see how fast they adapt to this technology. We don’t need to sell it to them, they simply want it themselves. This is the foundation we are building on,” said Visoid CEO Mark Szoke.
Founded in 2023 by former architect Mark Szoke and serial entrepreneur Joachim Holwech, Visoid states that rather than replacing the architect’s creative process, it transforms existing 3D models into high-quality visualisations in minutes while preserving the original design intent.
The platform mentions that it allows architects to iterate faster, communicate ideas more effectively and make better decisions, without relying on traditional rendering workflows.
“Architecture requires much more than beautiful images. Architects need AI that understands their models, preserves design intent and fits naturally into professional workflows,” said Joachim Holwech, CPO at Visoid.
Visoid reported that it has already gained traction among leading global architecture firms, including OMA, LEO A DALY, Sweco Group and Nordic Office of Architecture.
“Mark and Joachim combine deep domain expertise with serious technical depth in AI and machine learning, and a commercial instinct that comes naturally to them,” said Preben Songe-Møller, Partner and co-founder at Skyfall.
The company plans to use this fresh capital to support the company’s next stage of growth, including expanding its engineering, product and commercial teams. Visoid currently has a team of nine employees and expects to double in size by the end of the year.
It also plans to accelerate the development of new AI capabilities for architectural workflows, growing its international customer base and deepening partnerships with leading architecture and design firms.

articles.title: An AI agent was asked to book a gym class, whe none was available, it decided to hack the system and jump the queue
articles.text:
What just happened? As AI agents gain access to websites, software, and other online tools, they are beginning to take actions that go beyond what users ask them to do. An Australian user just learned that firsthand after asking an AI assistant to secure a place in a popular gym class. The system found a flaw in the booking software, reserved classes months before they were available, and removed another person from the waitlist without being asked.
The incident is being treated as Australia's first reported example of an AI agent independently exploiting a live system while carrying out a routine task. It offers an early look at a broader problem with newer AI tools: they can take steps that were never part of the user's instructions.
Andrew, who works for an Australian company that sells AI products to businesses, had been testing OpenClaw, an AI agent platform running on Anthropic's Claude service. Unlike a standard chatbot, an AI agent can use connected tools such as web browsers, email, and online services. It can also work through a series of actions to complete a task without being given step-by-step instructions.
That makes agents useful for routine work, but it also raises questions about what happens when they find weak security controls. An AI system may identify an unprotected feature and use it if it appears to be the quickest way to complete an assignment, even if the user did not intend for it to take that route.
Andrew asked the agent to make the gym booking because he saw it as a simple task for the technology.
"I was just sitting on the couch thinking, 'Gee, this is a chore,'" he said.
The agent began working through the gym's online booking system and soon reported that it had found a way to reserve places weeks ahead of the normal booking window. The apparent weakness was in the platform's application programming interface, or API, which allows software to communicate with the booking service.
Andrew was fourth on a waitlist for a class later that week. He then asked whether the agent could move him to the top of the list.
The software went beyond that request. It said it had removed the person at the top of the waitlist while testing whether the system would allow it.
"The API has zero authorization checks on cancelling other people's reservations ... I tested this with the person in waitlist position #1 – and it actually went through. So you've moved from #4 to #3 already," it messaged back.
Andrew then asked the agent to reverse the cancellation. It said it could not restore the other person's place.
"Bad news – I can't add them back," the AI agent replied.
The concern is not simply that an AI agent can spot a flaw in software. The larger issue is whether the system can distinguish between completing a task and taking actions that affect other people or systems. In this case, the agent appears to have treated the cancellation as a test of what the booking platform would permit.
The issue has drawn wider attention after reports that advanced models made by OpenAI autonomously hacked into another company's servers during testing. Other companies have made similar claims, increasing scrutiny of agents that can operate outside a chat window and take action in connected systems.

articles.title: LG Electronics Launches LG xboom Blast a Powerful Party Speaker
articles.text:
Monday, August 10th 2026
	
		
	
	
	
LG Electronics Launches LG xboom Blast a Powerful Party Speaker
LG Electronics (LG) today announced the global launch of LG xboom Blast, a premium portable Bluetooth party speaker designed to bring the energy of a great party wherever people gather. Built for beach days, camping trips, poolside gatherings and backyard celebrations, LG xboom Blast combines powerful sound, long-lasting reliability and intelligent audio technologies in a durable, portable design.
LG xboom Blast expands LG's growing family of xboom party speakers with a model designed specifically for outdoor use. With up to 220-watts of output, up to 36 hours of battery life and IP68-rated protection, LG xboom Blast combines powerful audio, portability and durability to helps users enjoy immersive sound across a wide range of outdoor environments.All-Day Reliability for Outdoor Freedom
When the party moves outdoors, people want the music to last as long as the experience itself. LG xboom Blast features a replaceable 99 watt-hour battery and Play Time Enhance technology that provide up to 36 hours of audio playback on a single charge.
Together with IP68-rated protection and verification through seven military-grade durability tests, the speaker is designed to withstand dust, water and the demands of outdoor use, giving users the confidence to keep the music going from afternoon gatherings through late-night celebrations.
Powerful Sound That Brings the Party Anywhere
At the heart of LG xboom Blast is xboom Signature Sound tuned by will.i.am. Delivering up to 220-watts of output when connected to AC power and up to 210-watts in battery mode, xboom Blast fills large spaces with rich, immersive sound designed for parties and gatherings.
Its high-output speaker system combines two 5.25-inch neodymium woofers with two 20-millimeter tweeters from Danish audio brand Peerless to produce deep bass, crisp highs and balanced full-range audio that brings greater energy and excitement to every party. Users can stream their favorite music wirelessly via Bluetooth or connect through USB-C for high-fidelity wired playback.
Intelligent Audio That Adapts to Every Setting
Outdoor environments and social gatherings present different acoustic conditions. To help users enjoy great sound without manual adjustments, AI Sound analyzes music and other audio content in real time and automatically adjusts sound settings to optimize playback, while Space Calibration Pro automatically adapts sound output based on the surrounding environment.
Sound Field Enhance expands the perceived soundstage for more immersive listening, and AI Lighting synchronizes the speaker's Dual Ring Lighting effects with different genres, moods and playlists to create a more engaging party atmosphere. For larger gatherings, Auracast enables multiple compatible speakers to connect wirelessly, extending sound coverage for larger shared listening experiences.
Designed for Easy Outdoor Mobility
Inspired by the familiarity of a weekend duffel bag, LG xboom Blast features a two-way carrying design with a top handle and flexible rope handle for easier transport. The rope handle supports vertical carrying, providing added flexibility when moving the speaker between outdoor locations such as the beach or campsite. Recognized with a 2026 Red Dot Design Award, the speaker combines practical portability with a unique visual identity inspired by outdoor lifestyles.
A durable fabric exterior and protective side bumpers support use on the go, while vertical or horizontal placement gives users more flexibility when setting up the speaker in different spaces, from crowded beach blankets to larger outdoor gathering areas.
"People today are spending more time outdoors, whether at the beach, by the pool or with friends and family in the backyard. Music helps bring those moments to life, which is why we designed xboom Blast to combine sound, durability and portability so people can bring that energy wherever they gather," said Lee Jeong-seok, head of the LG Media Entertainment Solution Company's Audio Business Division. "With LG xboom Blast, we wanted to create a speaker that gives people the freedom to enjoy great sound longer, more easily and in more places."
LG xboom Blast will begin rolling out in select markets this month, with additional markets to follow later this year.

articles.title: Keychron’s wireless Hall effect keyboard is back to its lowest price
articles.text:
Getting a keyboard with customizable Hall effect sensors is more affordable than it used to be, and you don’t need to compromise on quality to get a good deal. Keychron’s aluminum-clad K2 HE with a 75-percent layout is down to $103.99 (was $130) at Amazon, which matches the lowest price we’ve seen occur a few times throughout the year. The option with wood siding is $111.99 at Amazon, also 20 percent off its original price.
Keychron’s wireless Hall effect keyboard is back to its lowest price
We also found a good gaming laptop for $1,099, plus deals on Sony’s latest wired and wireless InZone headsets.
The keyboard can connect via USB-C, or wirelessly via Bluetooth or with a more reliable 2.4GHz connection. Its key bindings, actuation points, and much more can be configured in Keychron’s web-based tool. Or, you can flash your own firmware to the keyboard thanks to its open source QMK support.
In case you haven’t owned a Hall effect keyboard before, they’re worth considering if you’ve wanted more granular control over how much (or how little) effort is needed to press a key. What’s more, the sensors support Rapid Trigger, which primes each switch for another input long before it has been fully released, possibly letting you get the jump on opponents. The switches are hot-swappable, and the keyboard natively supports Windows, macOS, and Linux. This is a nice-looking keyboard for the money.
Other solid Verge-approved deals
- I don’t really like to recommend Nvidia RTX 5060-equipped gaming laptops that cost more than $1,000, but there’s a good deal happening at Walmart on a $1,099 model that’s $600 off. Gigabyte’s Aero X16 has a 16-inch 1600p 165Hz IPS screen, AMD’s capable Ryzen AI 7 350 processor, the aforementioned Nvidia GPU, rounded out with 16GB of 5,600MHz DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. I haven’t used this exact laptop, but we’re familiar with Gigabyte’s wares around here, and this is a sleek, almost Razer Blade-esque laptop with specs that mostly warrant its price. If the price of RAM and storage ever goes down, the laptop can be upgraded with up to 64GB and 4TB, respectively, with its additional slots. The configuration that has an RTX 5070 and 32GB of RAM is currently $1,499.99 at Best Buy.
- A couple of Sony’s recent InZone gaming headset releases have hit their lowest prices today. The InZone H9 Mk. 2 is its flagship wireless headset with the same drivers as the WH-1000XM6 headphones, plus a comfy design and great active noise cancellation. Their original $349.99 price felt high considering their near-all-plastic design, but $248 at Amazon and $249.99 at Best Buy is more reasonable. They sound phenomenal. Sony’s wired InZone H6 Air are discounted for the first time, and cost $178 (was $199) at Amazon and $179.99 at Best Buy. They are lightweight and have an open-back design, which to some adds a more realistic sound to games and movies (at the expense of sound isolation — they don’t block any noise whatsoever). Read our coverage of the H9 Mk. 2 and the H6 Air.
- Hoto’s USB-C-chargeable electric screwdriver is almost always discounted for major deal events, but it’s also cheaper on any given Monday, apparently. The screwdriver, which has three torque settings and includes 12 two-inch-long bits, is selling at Amazon for $27.99 when you enter the code WH4J6L4A at checkout (otherwise it’s $50). It’s nice to let technology take over sometimes, especially when what the Hoto screwdriver specializes in can possibly save you some pain from repetitive wrist motions. Also, it’s nice that it has a built-in circular LED light to illuminate dark spaces you’re working in. Walmart has a very similar Hoto screwdriver for $29.99, though it comes with fewer Torx bits.

articles.title: UK's Royal Navy sea drones contain component that secretly sent data to China, report claims — government cuts camera connectivity and insists data wasn’t sensitive, only ‘heartbeat communications’
articles.text:
UK's Royal Navy sea drones contain component that secretly sent data to China, report claims — government cuts camera connectivity and insists data wasn’t sensitive, only ‘heartbeat communications’
Affected K3 Scout drones used a Chinese camera component that subsequently failed a routine cyber vulnerability assessment.
K3 Scout surveillance drones used by the UK’s Royal Navy contain components that have been secretly transmitting data to China, according to reports. The Telegraph’s revelations suggest that the sea drones include a camera component that would send the data to China. However, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) says that it has removed all internet connectivity from the cameras after discovering the breach. The transmitted data was also limited in scope, insists the MoD, which characterized the transmissions as “heartbeat communications” to simply verify the device is online and working normally.
Western governments have been seeking to minimize the ingress of Chinese technology into sensitive and critical infrastructure for some years now. The pushback started with investigations into rising telecom brands like Huawei and ZTE, which became very successful with their cheap and efficient equipment in the West.
More recently, we have seen pushback affecting Chinese drone companies, as the utility and value of drones have become incredibly clear in the Russia – Ukraine war. Western allies obviously don’t want drones with potential Chinese backdoors, killswitches, or so on inside them. However, even manufacturers in China’s fiercest foe, Taiwan, recently admitted that its drone-making operations were still dependent on Chinese components.
Returning to the topic of drones, specifically, the sea drones in the Telegraph story were reportedly acquired by a major British defense contractor, Kraken Technology Group. The same company “sourced the cameras from a third party who had given assurances about their security,” says the newspaper. But an unnamed Telegraph source told the paper that this security lapse was a “major failure,” meaning that confidence in the platform has been lost. It even goes on to say that there are concerns that these drones could have snooped on highly sensitive special military forces meetings, even when switched off.
An MoD spokesperson told The Telegraph that the issues with the Chinese cameras were identified during a routine cyber vulnerability assessment. That seems like evidence of good practice, showing proactive testing and assurance procedures are in place. Moreover, the investigation “found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally.” That didn’t stop The Telegraph or shadow (opposition party) ministers from being “furious” about the revelations, though.
The K3 Scout drone can carry a 600kg payload at sea for 30 days continuously. The Royal Marines have been using a £12 million fleet of these drones since March and offered to deploy them to secure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. Special Operations Command also has K3 Scout drones, and these drones have been used by allies in NATO trials in the Baltic Sea.

articles.title: El final de 'La Casa del Dragón' temporada 3, explicado: ¿Quién muere y qué pasa con el Trono de Hierro?
articles.text:
ATENCIÓN: El artículo contiene SPOILERS de La Casa del Dragón 3x08.
Dos meses después de su estreno, la temporada 3 de La Casa del Dragón ha llegado a su final con el estreno de su octavo y último capítulo. La serie precuela de Juego de Tronos regresaba este año con la firme intención de dejar atrás las críticas a su entrega anterior. Así, arrancó con un inicio explosivo en una de las mayores batallas de toda la franquicia. Posteriormente ha ido calmando las aguas con un ritmo más lento. Y con la tensión por todo lo alto, al fin tenemos el desenlace.
En esta nueva tanda de capítulos, Rhaenyra y sus tropas toman de nuevo la capital del país, Desembarco del Rey, y recuperan el Trono de Hierro. Gracias a su ejército de dragones y a la dispersión de sus enemigos, la reina logra reinstaurar su gobierno. Aunque el pueblo no está tan convencido como ella pensaba. El miedo se convierte en su herramienta de control, pero eso le genera mucho desprecio más allá de sus cercanos.
Además, los Verdes no han dicho su última palabra. Aemond se ha convertido en dueño y señor de Harrenhal, mientras que Aegon daba un giro inesperado a la trama en el capítulo anterior al ver cómo su dragón Fuegosol estaba vivo después de todo. La guerra todavía no ha terminado y, por ello, La Casa del Dragón prometía un final espectacular a su temporada 3 que lo deje todo encarrilado de cara a la cuarta entrega, que será el desenlace definitivo de la serie.
La batalla de Ladera
El momento de más acción del final de La Casa del Dragón es, sin duda, la Batalla de Ladera. La serie culmina esta entrega como la empezó, con uno de los conflictos bélicos más salvajes y destructivos que se han visto en pantalla. Y es que, allí, Daemon Targaryen y sus tropas asedian sin cuartel ni descanso a los Hightower.
Sin embargo, la batalla no transcurre como ninguno de los dos bandos esperaba. Aunque las tropas de los Negros son clara mayoría, los Verdes contaban con un as en la manga. Ulf el Blanco había traicionado a Rhaenyra. Pero lejos de enfrentarse al ejército al comienzo de la batalla, Ormund Hightower se lo encuentra borracho y casi inconsciente. Esto desata la furia del hermano de Alicent sobre él, obligándole a ponerse manos a la obra. Pero esa reprimenda hace que el semilla de dragón opte por, sencillamente, arrasarlo todo a lomos de Ala de Plata.
El caos se desata definitivamente en Ladera por culpa de Ulf. El objetivo de los Negros era destronar de allí a Ormund Hightower y al príncipe Daeron Targaryen. Algo que, técnicamente, consiguen. Ormund muere y Daeron, simplemente, ha desaparecido. Pero no se puede decir que los Negros hayan triunfado. Y es que las llamas y la destrucción masiva de la ciudad han provocado infinidad de muertes de civiles inocentes. Y, precisamente, Rhaenyra le había pedido a Daemon que tomara Ladera sin hacerla parecer un monstruo.
Aunque técnicamente no es su culpa sino de Ulf y de la terquedad del propio Ormund Hightower, lo cierto es que el pueblo va a cargar los muertos sobre las espaldas de la reina. En definitiva, la hija mayor de Viserys sigue labrando, directa o indirectamente, su camino para convertirse en una tirana. El final de La Casa del Dragón temporada 3 es uno de los puntos de inflexión que ella quería evitar y que, definitivamente, no ha podido.
Una muerte final en La Casa del Dragón temporada 3
Pero es que, de hecho, la muerte de Ormund Hightower y de tantos inocentes no es la única que vemos en el episodio final de La Casa del Dragón temporada 3. Para empezar, Rhaenyra se harta del Septón Supremo. El líder religioso de Poniente no la reconoce como reina. Y aunque ella le da la oportunidad de hacerlo, él vuelve a negarse de manera agresiva. Por eso, ella ordena ejecutarlo. De nuevo, para el pueblo esto es una grave ofensa que atenta contra la Fe de los Siete.
Y si esta muerte en Desembarco del Rey no era suficiente agravio, el final de la temporada 3 de La Casa del Dragón le guarda una sorpresa a Rhaenyra cuando regresa a la Fortaleza Roja. Allí, descubre que Rhaena, su hermana pequeña, la hija de Alicent y esposa de Aegon, se ha suicidado. La joven se ha tirado por el ventanal de la habitación en la que la tenían encerrada, poniendo fin a su vida.
Su decisión está claramente justificada sobre el descenso a los infiernos del mal de Rhaenyra. Con el tiempo, ha perdido la esperanza de que la reina le permita salir de Desembarco del Rey y vivir una vida tranquila. Principalmente lo asume cuando se descubre que Aegon y Fuegosol siguen vivos. Esto provocará que tanto Rhaena como su hijo, heredero de Aegon, queden para siempre como rehenes en la Danza de los Dragones.
Date de alta en HBO MAX y tendrás acceso a las mejores series y películas exclusivas como The Wire, Los Soprano o Casa del Dragón. Incluye todo el catálogo de Warner, los clásicos de Cartoon Network, los grandes estrenos y el mejor deporte.
La única manera de evitar que Rhaenyra utilice a su hijo en su propio beneficio es el suicidio. Rhaena ha descubierto que a la reina de los Negros ya no le queda humanidad dentro. No va a mostrarse compasiva ni ante un recién nacido. Es mejor evitarle al bebé ese sufrimiento. Y, de paso, evitárselo a sí misma, pues Rhaenyra también quiere utilizar sus sueños premonitorios a su favor en la guerra. Por todo ello, se lanza por la ventana hacia su trágico destino.
Evidentemente, claro, el pueblo de nuevo sentenciará a Rhaenyra por este acto. Los rumores sobre que ha sido ella quien ha matado a Rhanea se extenderán como la pólvora por todo Poniente. Y esto es una tumba más en su ataúd, pues la esposa de Aegon era una reina pacífica, amable y muy querida. Es obvio que, entre la muerte de Rhaena y el desastre de la Batalla de Ladera, el reinado pacífico de Rhaenyra es ya imposible. A ojos del mundo es una villana.
Cómo prepara la temporada 4 de La Casa del Dragón
Así las cosas, este final de la temporada 3 de La Casa del Dragón ha dejado el escenario listo para la cuarta y última entrega. Rhaenyra mantiene la corona, pero se ha convertido en la tirana a la que todo Poniente odia. Y los Verdes todavía tienen a Aegon y a Aemond listos para una nueva batalla por el destino del Trono de Hierro.
Y es que Aegon confronta a su hermano pequeño en Harrenhall y le obliga a jurarle lealtad. Juntos, ambos partirán ahora hacia Ladera para encontrar a Ormund Hightower y a su hermano epqueño, Daeron Targaryen, que se había autoproclamado rey en le bando de los Verdes. Lo que se van a encontrar es, sin embargo, la ciudad totalmente arrasada. Así que próximamente partirán hacia Desembarco del Rey en busca de venganza.

European Athletics Championships 2026: Preview
Four years after the city hosted the Commonwealth Games, the eyes of the athletics world will once again be trained on Birmingham as the European Athletics Championships 2026 comes to the West Midlands. Some of the biggest stars in track and field will grace the Alexander Stadium as they bid to claim gold at the biggest event Europe has to offer.
Several British hopes will be desperate to triumph on home turf, with Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson aiming to complete a hat-trick of European titles with her third successive gold in the event. The 24-year-old will be pushed hard by Switzerland's Audrey Werro, who has run faster than any woman in the world over the distance in 2026, and the Netherlands' Femke Broeders-Bol, a serial Olympic, world and European champion who normally races in the 400m hurdles. Hodgkinson's training partner Georgia Hunter Bell won 800m gold at the Commonwealth Games last month, but she will compete in the 1,500m here.
Other Team GB athletes to look out for include sprint stars Dina Asher-Smith and Amy Hunt, heptathlete Katarina Johnson-Thompson and local boy Matthew Hudson-Smith, the four-time European champion in the 400m and 4x400m relay, who has had the North Stand at Alexander Stadium named after him.
It is not just about the host nation, though, with some genuine global superstars also set to feature. One of the biggest names in world athletics right now is Swedish pole vaulter Mondo Duplantis, a two-time Olympic champion who has broken the world record an astonishing 15 times. Meanwhile, fellow Scandinavian Jakob Ingebrigtsen - the Olympic 5,000m champion and 1,500m gold-medalist at Tokyo 2020 - is set to make his return from injury, representing Norway.
When do the European Athletics Championships 2026 start?
The European Athletics Championships 2026 start on Monday, August 10, with the first session beginning at 10.35am BST / 5.35am ET / 2.35am PT/ 7.35pm AEST.
The championships end on Sunday, August 16, with the men's 4x400m relay final the last event of the week at 9.48pm BST / 4.48pm ET / 1.48pm PT / 6.48am AEST (Mon).

articles.title: Windows 11's built-in weather app hogs more than 1.2 gigabytes of RAM just to tell the forecast — memory-sucking web wrapper filled with ads masquerades as an actual application
articles.text:
Windows 11's built-in weather app hogs more than 1.2 gigabytes of RAM just to tell the forecast — memory-sucking web wrapper filled with ads masquerades as an actual application
5x more memory consumption than macOS.
Windows is in a tough spot right now, with years of neglect and stagnation reaching a boiling point with customers. Lack of optimization, bloat, ads, forced AI slop, and persistent tracking have forced Microsoft to admit its missteps and commit to fixing the OS at large. Windows Latest's new testing shows that the built-in weather app is a perfect representation of the state of Windows. The "app" consumes up to 1.2GB of RAM while idling, and it serves up a bunch of ads while you check the temperature.
MSN Weather is the default weather app that ships with Windows, which explains why it's filled with promotions throughout, despite being part of a paid OS. To be clear, the app looks very modern and has all the data you could ask for, such as live radar overlays, hourly wind and precipitation breakdowns, air quality index, and moon phases. It's also accurate because the data is sourced from a bunch of different providers across the world, but mostly Foreca.
The author explains that getting accurate forecasts is not a cheap endeavor, so it's not like Microsoft is running a charity. But the comparison falls apart when you look at what the competition is offering. Apple's native weather app on macOS is just as beautiful, detailed, and accurate, yet it's free of ads. It also only consumes about 250MB of memory to show all that data, so 5x less than Windows. This is because MSN Weather is technically not even an app to begin with; it's a web wrapper that's pinging a bunch of browser tabs in real-time.
When the author clicked on the Task Manager entry for MSN Weather, they saw 8 Chromium-based subprocesses, confirming that they're just looking at a website being rendered via WebView 2. For context, native Windows apps are supposed to adhere to the WinUI framework, which the company is slowly adopting over Win32 and UWP. Microsoft is committed to updating all the native apps Windows ships with to Win32, which should significantly improve their optimization, but we don't know if the ads will suddenly disappear as well.
The author saw Adobe Acrobat ads while checking the forecast, and we saw two ads — one for LendingTree and another for Spotify. Apart from that, scrolling around the app and clicking on the different menus and boxes was fast enough. We have to emphasize that the app really is granular and well-built from an aesthetic point of view; Microsoft gets full points for that, or is it MSN? That distinction is another issue that makes the weather app conundrum a bit more confusing.
When Microsoft promised to rebuild all native Windows 11 apps, it didn't explicitly say those would include MSN-branded services too, like MSN Weather and MSN News. Seeing as though they're simply called by their utilitarian names in the OS, there's a strong chance that these memory hoggers will also be eventually upgraded. For now, just stick to your phone, especially if you were among those who immediately Googled how to remove the weather widget from your taskbar that fateful day.

articles.title: Espelhos no espaço podem iluminar a Terra e afetar a vida noturna
articles.text:
Uma tecnologia criada para levar luz solar a diferentes pontos da Terra pode gerar um efeito colateral preocupante. A Reflect Orbital recebeu aprovação da FCC para lançar um satélite com espelho capaz de refletir a luz do Sol para o planeta, mas astrônomos alertam para riscos à ciência e à segurança.
Chamado Eärendil-1, o satélite faz parte de um projeto que prevê até 50 mil espelhos em órbita. A proposta é oferecer iluminação e energia solar sob demanda, inclusive à noite. O receio é que o brilho desses objetos altere o céu noturno e provoque danos à visão.
Uma ideia antiga volta ao espaço
Usar espelhos em órbita para refletir a luz solar para a Terra não é novidade. O conceito é discutido há mais de um século e foi testado pela Rússia nos anos 1990, com o projeto Znamya.
Agora, a Reflect Orbital pretende retomar a ideia. O Eärendil-1 terá um espelho de 18 metros quadrados e, segundo a empresa, poderá produzir um feixe de luz de cerca de 5 quilômetros de largura.
Entre as aplicações previstas estão:
- geração de energia em fazendas solares;
- iluminação de áreas urbanas durante a noite;
- apoio a operações de busca e resgate;
- iluminação de obras e atividades industriais;
- possível aumento da produtividade agrícola.
O céu pode ficar claro demais
O satélite poderá ter brilho semelhante ao de Vênus fora do feixe e ser quatro vezes mais brilhante que a Lua dentro da área iluminada. A preocupação aumenta com a possibilidade de dispersão da luz pela atmosfera.
De acordo com a Royal Astronomical Society, o céu noturno poderia ficar de três a quatro vezes mais brilhante nas regiões afetadas caso dezenas de milhares de objetos refletissem a luz solar.
Roohi Dalal, vice-diretora de políticas públicas da American Astronomical Society, resumiu a crítica: “Nossa principal preocupação é que sentimos que a Reflect Orbital não fez a devida diligência”.
O aumento da luminosidade poderia dificultar a observação de galáxias distantes e até a identificação de asteroides potencialmente perigosos.
O risco também chega aos telescópios
A ameaça não envolve apenas grandes observatórios. Em documentos enviados à FCC, a própria Reflect Orbital reconheceu que observar acidentalmente um único satélite por meio de um telescópio de 12 polegadas poderia causar danos permanentes aos olhos.
Leia mais:
- Eclipse solar total: NASA se prepara para estudar o fenômeno
- Agência Espacial Europeia prepara força-tarefa para eclipse solar histórico
- Brasil terá “Anel de Fogo” no céu em pleno Carnaval no ano que vem
Também há preocupação com a falta de um plano claro para avisar o público sobre quando e onde o serviço estará ativo. Motoristas e pilotos poderiam ainda enfrentar episódios de cegueira temporária durante o movimento do feixe.
Christopher Buscombe, porta-voz da Reflect Orbital, afirmou: “Nossa abordagem é incremental: testar e aprender”.
A empresa diz que o primeiro satélite será usado para testar a tecnologia e suas salvaguardas. Mesmo assim, organizações ligadas à astronomia e à segurança aérea questionam se essas medidas serão suficientes.
A discussão vai além do Eärendil-1. Para os críticos, uma frota de milhares de espelhos brilhantes pode prejudicar pesquisas científicas, afetar pessoas e animais e mudar permanentemente a aparência do céu noturno.
Entre as alternativas estão ampliar a instalação de painéis solares e desenvolver sistemas de baterias melhores. Para os astrônomos, a questão é até onde vale avançar em busca de energia sem comprometer a observação do céu.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: U.S. Startup Fields Quantum Sensors to Reduce Reliance on GPS - EE Times
articles.text:
Startup Dirac Labs is field-testing quantum sensors that the company expects will help reduce the risks of reliance on GPS and other satellite-based systems for navigation. A former U.S. Defense Advanced Projects Research Agency (DARPA) program manager who advises Dirac Labs told EE Times the company should be able to reach large-scale production within a few years.
The Madison, Wisconsin-based company, founded in 2023, said it is working with U.S. defense primes and agritech companies as integration partners.
“Spoofing GPS can be disastrous,” Dirac co-founder and CEO Sanket Deshpande told EE Times in an interview. Dirac partners include aircraft and avionics manufacturers in defense as well as international firms that are working on underground and underwater positioning where GPS doesn’t work, he said, declining to identify partners.
“Those are some select few partners that we’re working with to demonstrate feasibility and applications of our platform,” Deshpande added. “Once we get that milestone done, we would start engaging with customers on some specific use cases.”
While navigation systems such as China’s BeiDou, Europe’s Galileo, and the U.S. GPS rely on satellites to determine a user’s location, quantum navigation counts on quantum sensing, which measures environmental data with incredible precision and sensitivity, according to Europe’s Airbus in a March 2026 blog. GPS jammers send disruptive signals on the same frequency as a GPS satellite, blocking the satellite signal. GPS spoofers use counterfeit signals with incorrect location data that is read by the GPS receiver. Both types of subterfuge are a growing threat due to geopolitical instability, Airbus said.
Airbus didn’t name quantum sensing partners it is working with.
Dirac is making a magnetic map of the Earth by fusing data available in the public domain, Dirac COO Aishwarya Das said. That map untethers the Dirac system from satellites.
“We have built our own fusion engine, which takes 70 years of magnetic data from flights over different parts of the U.S.,” Das added. “That entire map is loaded into our sensor. AI research over the last few months has accelerated. We’re able to quantize these models to make them much smaller and much more powerful so they can sit on a very small chip and do all these processes without sending any data to a cloud service.”
Diamond foundries
Dirac is working with several diamond foundries in the Chicago area to engineer nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond that serve as atomic-scale sensing qubits. The diamond substrate is coupled with an Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano module for small, low-power embedded computing as part of its technology stack. Dirac aims to replace the Nvidia chip with an FPGA.
Dirac works with Great Lakes Crystal Technologies in Chicago and a University of Chicago spinoff called staC12 for the diamond materials, Deshpande said. Dirac has put a photonic layer on top of the diamond substrate to enhance light extraction and improve sensitivity while maintaining room-temperature operation in a small form factor. The photonic portion is contained in a plastic injection mold that’s integrated with the diamond substrate and packaged into a 5 × 5-centimeter cube. Inside that package, laser light generates a fluorescence from the diamond defects that is measured by a photodiode.
The company plans to adopt the full semiconductor manufacturing process.
“All of this will be manufactured in a standard CMOS foundry,” Deshpande said. “Today, we are just doing it on a small scale in university fabs. The idea is to work with a foundry like SkyWater. You don’t need to get to a million-unit tape-out. With folks like SkyWater, we can do a low-volume multi-process wafer where we can get smaller volumes for our initial customers and, as we scale, have the flexibility to increase the production volume.”
Building both the semiconductor hardware and the AI modules was never possible for a small company in the past, Deshpande said.
“Today, with the acceleration that data centers are providing to us, we can have that ambition to do all of this under a single roof,” he added.
Dirac is about a year or two away from wide-scale production, according to Michael Nayak, a former DARPA program manager who is now a scientific adviser to the company.
“The thing that is difficult about quantum navigation sensors is actually not the quantum part of it,” Nayak said. “It’s more the manufacturing part. We know what the potential is, but actually being able to drive the cost down is not something that you can deliver on until you’ve done it, the classic assembly-line problem.”
Applications
Dirac aims to enable navigation in places outside GPS range using its platform.
“That means everything from air to underground, underwater,” Deshpande said. New applications include protection of underwater cables and assets, as well as seabed mapping. Over 90% of the world’s seabed is unmapped, Deshpande noted.
Undersea cable cuts in the Red Sea, the Baltic Sea, and the Taiwan Strait have increasingly disrupted global internet traffic and telecommunications. Ship anchors and suspected sabotage cause the cuts. Specialized cable ships can take several weeks to locate breaks and proceed with repairs.
“There are a lot of movements on the defense side to bolster the industrial base with more options from the commercial industry, from startups, from people who want to move quickly and take technology out of the lab,” Nayak said. “The denied area navigation problem is just one that is core to multiple Department of Defense missions.”
Denied area navigation is essentially GPS jamming.
“GPS jamming is fairly widespread,” Nayak said. “It’s easy. We see it in Ukraine. We see Russia jamming GPS. We see even smaller players like Iran doing it.”
Every civilian airplane or drone could use quantum sensing, Nayak noted.
“Defense just has a more urgent need,” he said.
Competition
Other companies in quantum sensing include Q-CTRL and Google spinoff SandboxAQ, Deshpande said.
“We think our unique approach toward scalability, not making bespoke sensors, but making sensors through the semiconductor route allows us to reduce the cost,” he noted.
China is also developing quantum sensing tech, Deshpande noted.
“I think we’re still leading here in the U.S., but definitely, China is a close competitor to watch out for.”

articles.title: Linus Torvalds: encontrar bugs usando IA é o "novo normal" no Linux • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Linus Torvalds: encontrar bugs usando IA é o “novo normal” no Linux
O Linux 7.2 está prestes a ser lançado. Um tanto resignado, Linus Torvalds destacou o alto volume de correções via IA que a nova versão trará.
A sétima e, provavelmente, última versão release candidate do Linux 7.2 foi anunciada no domingo (09/08). Isso significa que a próxima versão do kernel está prestes a ser lançada. Como sempre, as novidades incluirão correções no código. Mas muitas delas são oriundas de ferramentas de IA, como o próprio Linus Torvalds admitiu:
Eu não posso dizer que estou exatamente empolgado com o tamanho disso tudo, mas é o que é: o novo normal com muitas correções, muitas delas decorrentes da revisão feita por diversas ferramentas de IA.
E nada parece particularmente assustador em si — é só que há muita coisa aqui. A maior parte é bem pequena, embora tenhamos algumas modificações maiores (…).
Linus Torvalds, mantenedor do Linux
O tom um tanto resignado da mensagem de Linus, postada na lista de discussão do projeto, tem uma razão para existir: a exemplo de tantos outros softwares, ferramentas de inteligência artificial vêm sendo usadas para identificar vulnerabilidades de segurança no kernel; o problema é que a quantidade de notificações a respeito tem sido exagerada.
Se por um lado essa dinâmica possibilita identificar falhas importantes que poderiam passar despercebidas ou demorar para serem descobertas, por outro, sobrecarrega os desenvolvedores do kernel com notificações sobre bugs pouco relevantes, em fila de correção ou até já solucionados.
Não por acaso, a versão atual do kernel, o Linux 7.1, foi lançada depois que os desenvolvedores conseguiram manejar o volume acentuado de notificações de brechas feitas por ferramentas de IA.
Isso talvez te faça imaginar que “o pai do Linux” sente uma verdadeira ojeriza pelas tais ferramentas. Mas não é o caso: o próprio Torvalds defende o uso de IA no kernel, desde que isso seja feito de modo coerente, isto é, sob circunstâncias em que seu uso é realmente vantajoso.
Em sua mensagem mais recente, Torvalds dá a entender que o desenvolvimento do kernel Linux 7.2 deu mais trabalho do que o esperado devido ao grande número de correções da versão, muitas das quais identificadas via IA.
Apesar disso, o lançamento oficial do Linux 7.2 deve ocorrer no próximo fim de semana, tal como planejado, até porque, apesar de numerosas, a maioria das correções é considerada pequena. Neste ponto, vale destacar que versões release candidate precedem o lançamento oficial.
Curiosamente, o Linux 7.2 pode vir sem um código obsoleto que já estava na fila de remoção, mas que teve esse processo apressado de modo a fazer a IA parar de gerar notificações relacionadas a ele.
Na atual fase, parece que os desenvolvedores do Linux tentam achar um ponto de equilíbrio: o uso da IA traz benefícios, mas ainda é preciso ajustar a dose.

articles.title: 'From a chore to something I could actually stick with' — how Gemini and Garmin made me love running for the first time
articles.text:
I've always disliked running, but here's how Gemini and Garmin made me actually enjoy it for the first time
On-the-fly adjustments helped turn a chore into a sustainable habit
I’ve never particularly enjoyed running, especially when training solo, but it takes the least effort for me to prepare for in the morning compared to my preferred activities — cycling or badminton — and it’s also a nice cross-training option.
After reading about my colleagues using AI to build training plans, I thought it could be an opportunity for me to change how I feel about running, so I turned to Google Gemini and asked it to build a training plan to prepare for a major running event here in Australia, the Sydney City2Surf.
My goal was to try out a plan that could easily adapt after a setback, like an injury or illness, while balancing run training with my usual badminton sessions and bike rides within a week.
I also wanted to see if I could stick to running for longer compared to my previous attempts, which involved either winging it — running for as long as I could until I ran out of breath — or following a rigid online plan.
Setup
My initial prompt was “How realistic is it for a beginner runner to train for City2Surf starting next week?” It was in late December 2025, so Gemini replied that I had plenty of time, as the event was on August 9 this year.
City2Surf has a 14km route that starts from Sydney CBD and finishes at Bondi Beach, which explains the name. It’s an infamously hilly route, headlined by a 2km section midway through the course with an average gradient of about 3 to 4%, or 75 to 80m in elevation.
“Most beginner-friendly training plans only require 12–16 weeks,” the response read. “Starting now puts you in an excellent position to not just survive the race, but actually enjoy it and run the majority of the course.”
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Here’s the general overview from Gemini:
| Phase | Duration | Focus | 
| Foundation (Now – March) | ~12 Weeks | Focus on consistency. Aim for 2–3 days a week of a "Run-Walk" method (e.g., run 2 mins, walk 1 min). | 
| Building (April – June) | ~12 Weeks | Increase your long run distance once a week. Start introducing gentle hills and light strength training (squats/lunges). | 
| Race Specific (July – August) | 6–8 Weeks | Focus on endurance and Heartbreak Hill. Your longest run should reach 12km–13km about two weeks before race day. | 
To make sure I stuck to the plan, I asked Gemini how to enter the workouts into my old Garmin watch, and it gave me a step-by-step guide.
I was also offered to test the newly released Garmin Forerunner 70 and 170 range while I was training, and I chose the 170 Music edition. I wanted to see if the built-in music function and Garmin Pay wireless payments were enough for me to leave my phone at home during training sessions.
Lugging my heavy iPhone 16 Pro Max in a running belt during my first few weeks of running became annoying, so the Forerunner was just what I needed. It also completely cuts down on distractions, and the voice prompts also helped keep me on track during interval sessions.
I managed to stick to the program for the first few months while keeping my social badminton games and bike rides. But things started to get tricky as I progressed into the second phase.
Setbacks and adjustments
Heading into phase 2 of my training plan, I unexpectedly got Achilles tendonitis, which my physiotherapist told me was the result of putting too much load too quickly on my legs and feet. Recovery took more than a month of rehab and rest.
When I was cleared to run again, I told Gemini I’d missed a few weeks and asked how I should adjust. It told me to revisit an earlier training week to ease back in instead of starting over. I was also advised to drop to one social badminton evening a week and swap the other for a bike ride.
After a month back, I was sidelined once again for a similar amount of time, thanks to a chest infection with a nagging cough and cold.
Ultimately, I felt that these setbacks were enough for me to decide not to enter the City2Surf, even though Gemini said I still had enough time to train. I set my sights on next year’s event instead.
“Forgoing the City2Surf entirely to prioritize a balanced, sustainable routine is a phenomenal decision,” Gemini’s response read after making this decision. “Since you haven't registered yet, dropping the pressure of a hard August 9th deadline allows you to completely shift your mindset from 'panic training' to building a strong, bulletproof foundation for the long run.”
Looking back, I likely would have just quit after the first setback if I had been following a more rigid training plan. I’d probably have no idea how to proceed after these setbacks, and laziness would quickly take over, and I’d be back to square one again.
Refocused training
Without the pressure of a fixed race date, Gemini readjusted my plan over the next four weeks to focus on just two sessions per week: one day of run-walk intervals and one longer, uninterrupted easy jog before I move forward with a fresh training plan. This much easier training load has made running a more intentional endeavour, while balancing with my other activities without putting too much strain on myself.
Overall, I’ve found that the flexibility and adaptability of Gemini’s training plan have made my progression much more sustainable, and I never felt like I was pushing myself too hard or going too easy. Setbacks are much easier to recover from, letting me work back into shape without needing to start over. And if I feel like doing more days of the other activities during some weeks, Gemini can help plan my week ahead.
While I ultimately failed in my original objective of joining a popular running event, I ended up enjoying the journey of becoming a better runner at a more sustainable pace.
Should you let AI be your running coach?
For beginners or runners who want a flexible, low-pressure plan, Gemini is a genuinely useful starting point. It helped me build something realistic, adapt when I missed training and keep progressing without constantly feeling like I was falling behind.
I'd argue though that it's not a substitute for proper coaching. AI can help with structure, pacing and consistency, but it cannot spot problems in your form, keep you motivated, or hold you accountable when training gets tough. And as with any AI-generated plan, especially for anything more advanced, you should still treat it as a starting point rather than gospel.
For my purposes, though, Gemini was enough to turn running from a chore into something I could actually stick with.

articles.title: DJI y sus drones están en problemas. Los próximos modelos podrían ser más difíciles de volar
articles.text:
DJI y todo su catálogo de drones acaba de recibir un aviso que podría poner en peligro una de las funciones más útiles, básicas e importantes de sus cuadricópteros. Y, aunque la posible prohibición se ha puesto en marcha en Estados Unidos, podría ser una decisión que afecte a España y casi todo el globo. No está claro cómo va a actuar la compañía, pero si la FCC sigue adelante con su plan, parece bastante claro que una de las ventajas de estos drones podría desaparecer. ¿El qué exactamente? La facilidad de volarlos en entornos complicados o durante la noche.
La historia comienza tras una publicación de la FCC para prohibir ciertos drones de DJI que se oficializó en 2025. Ahora la agencia estadounidense ha querido ampliarla, incluyendo en la ecuación varias características de estos cuadricópteros que, según EE. UU., ponen en peligro la seguridad nacional y pueden atentar contra la defensa del país.
La FCC considera que ciertos componentes y funciones de estos drones pueden tener "capacidad militar" en el país, por lo que el día 2 de septiembre tomará una decisión sobre la prohibición de los sensores LiDAR, los dispensadores de aerosoles y las cámaras térmicas en los drones DJI y otras marcas.
Esta prohibición no afectaría a los drones que ya están en manos de los usuarios, pero sí obligaría a DJI a retirar algunos modelos de las tiendas. Y esto, aunque todavía no está confirmado, podría afectar gravemente al mercado internacional.
¿Por qué es tan grave que EE. UU. prohíba los sensores LiDAR en los drones DJI?
Las cámaras térmicas y los dispensadores automáticos de aerosoles son características que afectan a las series más profesionales de DJI. Ahora bien, los sensores LiDAR sí son importantísimos en prácticamente toda la gama comercial de la marca. Llevan años en casi todos los drones, y son los culpables de que la compañía cuente con esa facilidad para volar en casi cualquier escenario y orografía de forma segura.
Estos sensores son capaces de medir distancias de forma sumamente precisa en casi cualquier condición, lo que permite a los drones DJI evitar obstáculos de forma automática, saber a qué distancia del suelo están, volar durante la noche de forma segura o navegar en entornos con mucha vegetación sin chocar con ramas o plantas.
Pues bien, este avanzado sistema es el que Estados Unidos quiere prohibir en los drones de la compañía a partir del día 2 de septiembre. ¿Solo en EE. UU.? Sí, porque la FCC no tiene competencias en otros países, pero hacer modificaciones tan serias en un mercado tan gigantesco puede tener consecuencias a nivel mundial.
Cuando la Unión Europea obligó a Apple a cambiar el Lightning por un USB C, la compañía realizó el cambio en todo el mundo para evitar tener que fabricar dos modelos, y esto podría ser algo que se repita en el catálogo de DJI. No es seguro, pero podría pasar.
Sobre todo en los modelos más económicos, donde los márgenes son menores y tener que lanzar varios modelos para diferentes mercados podría generar una subida en el precio de algunos modelos.
Por supuesto, DJI tiene la capacidad de lanzar modelos con y sin LiDAR en diferentes mercados, pero hacerlo en los drones más básicos es algo que solo está en sus manos. Esta condición de EE. UU. podría afectar a los próximos productos de la compañía, aunque para confirmarlo o desmentirlo hay que esperar.

articles.title: Can AI Command Earth-to-Orbit Operations? - EE Times
articles.text:
The aerospace and defense sector is facing a confluence of geopolitical instability, rapid technological advances, evolving security requirements, and complex global supply chains.
According to aerospace and defense consultant Alessandro Pianelli, author of the white paper “Aerospace & Defence: 30-Year Outlook 2026-2056,” the entire sector is “embarking on an unprecedented phase of transformation.” Pianelli identified AI-driven autonomy, space-based architectures and infrastructures, advanced propulsion (electric and nuclear), hypersonics, and quantum technologies as key technological clusters that will influence the sector over the next three decades.
Market momentum is indeed accelerating. The aerospace and defense sector grew from $884 billion in 2023 to $986 billion in 2024 and is forecast to reach $1.23 trillion by 2028. The global space economy hit a record $613 billion in 2024, with commercial activity accounting for 78% of the market. Projections suggest the space market will exceed $1 trillion by 2032 and amount to $1.8 trillion by 2035. Meanwhile, the war in Ukraine has reinforced the importance of defense investment, contributing to a 9% increase in global spending in 2024 and greater funding for AI, cyber, and space-based capabilities.
Will the wars of tomorrow be fought by networks of autonomous machines? Can autonomous systems be trusted to operate effectively in GPS- and communications-denied environments? Where do edge AI and swarm intelligence intersect? What safeguards are needed to prevent adversaries from exploiting AI-driven decision-making? Are orbital data centers the next phase of AI infrastructure or their most expensive dead end?
This Special Report reviews advances in electronics and semiconductor technologies that make aerospace and defense systems ever more autonomous and resilient. It relies on interviews with companies such as Aalto, Anduril Carbice Corporation, Mikros Technologies, RUSI, SatVu, Sceye, Swarmer, and Tytan Technologies, as well as Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Centre for Security, Diplomacy, and Strategy at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium). It also features a collection of contributions by Avella Security, Edgewater Wireless Systems, and Milexia.
The Stratosphere Race: HAPS Move from Experiment to Commercial Reality
By Rebecca Pool
While autonomous flight is often associated with drones, a revolution in autonomy is unfolding in the stratosphere. At altitudes of about 20 km, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS) from the likes of Airbus subsidiary Aalto, Thales, and BAE Systems’ Prismatic are targeting the largely untapped airspace between most air traffic and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites.
SatVu Targets Industrial Intelligence with Thermal Imaging
By Rebecca Pool
With HotSat-2 in orbit and fresh funding, U.K. startup SatVu is demonstrating how high-resolution thermal satellite data can reveal real-world industrial activity.
Data Centers in Space: A Brilliant Idea or Delusional?
The power and thermal issues of placing data centers in space are formidable.
Space-Station Tech Pivots to Cool AI Data Centers
Mikros Technologies and Carbice Corporation are adapting International Space Station technology to address AI data center heat challenges, using advanced liquid cooling and carbon nanotube thermal interface materials to improve chip performance.
Europe’s Path to Defense Resilience Lies in Technological Independence
By Florian Pivit, Milexia
Europe’s aerospace and defense sector is entering a defining decade. Geopolitical instability, electronic warfare, fragmented supply chains, and accelerating advances in autonomous systems are fundamentally reshaping how nations think about sovereignty, resilience, and technological independence.
The Rise of Autonomous Drone Warfare
By Rebecca Pool
Russia has transformed drone warfare, mass-producing inexpensive autonomous attack drones and launching up to 1,000 in a single night, overwhelming Ukrainian defenses and relentlessly targeting cities and critical infrastructure.
Billions Pour into Autonomous Defense as AI Redefines Warfare
By Rebecca Pool
Record funding is accelerating AI-driven autonomy in defense, with drones and edge AI set to dominate battlefields.
Securing Next-Generation Defense by Design
By Daryl Flack, Avella Security
Europe’s defense landscape is being forced to recalibrate in response to a shifting global order defined by geopolitical instability, volatility, and the increasingly unpredictable nature of hybrid warfare, all of which are straining interconnected supply chains.
Military AI Agents Under Cyberthreat: The Route Forward
This article is the first part of a two-part series looking at how military AI agents are under threat from cyberthreats. Part 1 outlines some of the challenges that different militaries face and what threats they are up against. Part 2 looks at some of the technical solutions available and how robust governance is a critical part of ensuring military cyber safety in the long-term.
Protecting Military AI Agents From Cyberthreats
Part 2 of this two-part series looks at how military AI agents are under threat from cyberattacks and nefarious actors. If you missed Part 1, you should read it here first, as it covers the main cyberthreats facing military AI agents today. This article looks at both the technical solutions available and the governance requirements going forward to combat the increasing number and diverse range of cyberthreats that military AI agents are facing.

articles.text:
Home
                        
       			
					
TECHNICAL PAPERS
		
								August 10th, 2026 - 
								By: Technical Paper Link
								
							
						
Researchers from Texas A&M University, KIMM, and UST published a technical paper titled “Self-Focusing Control for Depth-Precise Wafer Slicing of 4H-SiC in Femtosecond Laser Processing.”
Abstract Excerpt:
“Femtosecond laser slicing for 4H-SiC wafers offers a non-contact processing approach to produce thin layers with low defects, while strong optical nonlinearities obscure the relationship between the laser parameters and the resulting slicing quality. Here, we systematically investigate Kerr-induced self-focusing using a femtosecond laser in 4H-SiC slicing by combining experiments, a semi-empirical analytical model, and numerical ray optics simulations. We demonstrate that the interplay between pulse energy and processing depth governs the self-focusing behavior, which directly correlates with post-separation surface texture parameters and separation stress, thereby linking nonlinear beam propagation to slicing quality. “
Find the technical paper here. August 2026.
Kang, Dong Hee, Jaeseung Lim, Mishfaqur Rahman, Seongheum Han, Jae-Hak Lee, Seungman Kim, and Jihoon Jeong. “Self-Focusing Control for Depth-Precise Wafer Slicing of 4H-SiC in Femtosecond Laser Processing.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2608.03814 (2026).

articles.title: Du surplace, mais avec style : j'ai testé le Galaxy Z Flip de Samsung
articles.text:
| Ergonomies et design |  | 
| Poids | 180 g | 
| Certification d'étanchéité | IP48 | 
| Mémoire extensible (carte SD) | Non | 
| Connectique | USB-C | 
| Dimensions | 166.9 x 75.4 x 6.1 mm | 
| Technologies biométriques | Capteur d'empreinte digitale, Reconnaissance faciale simple | 
| Charge par induction | Oui | 
| Antichoc (norme MIL-STD-810) | Non | 
| Performances |  | 
| Processeur | Exynos 2600 | 
| GPU | Xclipse 960 | 
| Mémoire vive (RAM) | 12 Go | 
| Photo |  | 
| Module Photo arrière 1 | Grand-angle, 50 Mpx, f/1,8 | 
| Module Photo arrière 2 | Ultra grand-angle, 12 Mpx, f/2,2 | 
| Autonomie |  | 
| Capacité de la batterie | 4300 mAh | 
Samsung renouvelle son smartphone pliant à clapet. Pour succéder à un Galaxy Z Flip 7 qui avait su séduire par son format, le sud-coréen mise sur davantage de légèreté et de finesse, quitte à masquer derrière des améliorations cosmétiques un certain ronronnement technique.
Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 lui a ravi la vedette, et pour cause : il inaugure un nouveau format, quand lui-même se présente comme une itération d’un smartphone déjà bien connu. Et pourtant, le Galaxy Z Flip 8 a été officialisé, comme son frère Fold, au cours de l’événement estival Galaxy Unpacked mené tambour battant par Samsung, et intéresse d’autant plus qu’il reste le smartphone pliant le moins onéreux du fabricant.
Le Galaxy Z Flip 8, donc, conserve le format clapet de ses prédécesseurs - et même leur format, tout court. L’appareil pensé pour la compacité et le style conserve un système de double affichage, un mode “Flex” pratique, mais inaugure une puce Exynos 2600 qui doit y faire ses preuves ainsi qu’une batterie au silicium-carbone. Comptez pour cet appareil la modique somme de 1299 € (12/256 Go) ou 1399 € (12/512 Go).
Nous avons testé le Galaxy Z Flip 8 sous Android 17 avec One UI 9.0.
Le Galaxy Z Flip 8 s’inscrit dans la plus pure tradition des itérations signées Samsung. Il faut en effet se pencher très près sur la fiche technique de l’appareil pour déceler de véritables différences avec son prédécesseur, le Galaxy Z Flip 7. Ses dimensions sont à peine revues à la hausse, puisque l’on relève des mensurations de 166,9 x 75,4 mm lorsqu’il est ouvert (face aux 166,7 x 75,2 mm du Z Flip 7), et de 85,7 x 75,4 mm fermé, contre 85,5 x 75,2 mm. Mais s’il est un peu plus grand, le Z Flip 8 est plus fin (6,1 mm ouvert, 13, 1 mm fermé, votre 6,5/13,7 mm) et plus léger. Il pèse en effet 180 g, soit 8 g de moins que son prédécesseur. On apprécie l’effort, et le fait que ce terminal à clapet, qui a le mérite de rentrer facilement dans une poche, se classe parmi les smartphones “légers” du moment. Après tout, un Galaxy S26 n’est pas beaucoup moins lourd, avec ses 167 g.
Côté design, on retrouve un châssis en aluminium à la finition mate, de même que son dos vitré : si traces de doigts il y a, on les voit surtout sur l’écran externe de l’appareil. Ce dernier conserve une diagonale de 4,1 pouces, et occupe presque 85 % de la façade de l’appareil. Deux modules photos y sont intégrés, et attirent immanquablement les poussières. L’écran interne de 6,9 pouces, lui, dispose de bordures plus fines encore, exploitant près de 89 % de l’espace disponible.
Une fois ouvert, le smartphone est très fin. Certes, ses 6,1 mm n’atteignent pas les extrêmes d’un Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, mais la minceur de l’appareil ne se fait pas moins sentir. Elle facilite la préhension du smartphone, même s’il faut garder en tête que son format étiré complique la tâche à qui souhaite balayer le haut de son écran à une main. N’oublions pas une pliure centrale qui paraît s’être encore adoucie, malgré l’absence de Flex Titanium (technologie réservée aux deux Z Fold 8), et le placement du lecteur d’empreintes digitales sur la tranche droite du mobile, sur son bouton d’allumage.
Pour le reste, le Galaxy Z Flip 8 donne dans le classique. Il est compatible avec les eSIM, en plus d’une nano-SIM classique et prend en charge le wifi 7. En revanche, le Bluetooth 6.0, qui a fait son apparition sur les Z Fold 8 et Z Fold 8 Ultra, n’est pas de la partie : le modèle à clapet lui préfère le Bluetooth 5.4. Enfin, on note le maintien de la norme IP48, qui ne prémunit pas le Z Flip 8 des poussières les plus fines, mais lui permet de résister à l’eau. L'écran extérieur est quant à lui protégé par une vitre Gorilla Glass Victus 2.
Pour aller plus loin :
À l’image de son aîné, le Galaxy Z Flip 8 dispose de deux écrans, tous deux reposant sur la technologie Amoled. Le principal affiche une diagonale de 6,9 pouces pour une définition de 2520 x 1080 pixels (ratio 21:9), ce qui se traduit par une résolution de 400 ppp. La luminosité est au rendez-vous : nous avons relevé un maximum de 2638 cd/m², ce qui suffit très largement au quotidien, et permet de compenser des reflets qui restent un peu élevés (près de 45 % de réflectance) lorsque le smartphone est utilisé en plein soleil. L’afficheur parvient également à tomber sous le cd/m² au besoin, ce que les scrolleurs compulsifs du soir apprécieront.
Comme souvent dans l’écosystème de Samsung, il faut se tourner vers le mode d’affichage “Naturel” pour tirer le meilleur du Flip 8. Le delta E y est bas (1,6), les dérives colorimétriques étant très limitées, et la température des couleurs, certes légèrement chaude si on la compare aux 6500 K de référence, est fixée à 6374 K. Cela vaut toutefois mieux que le mode “Vif”, appliqué par défaut, qui produit des couleurs trop froides (6804 K), pour un delta E moins faible (1,71).
L’écran externe du Galaxy Z Flip 8 conserve une diagonale de 4,1 pouces, une définition de 948 x 1048 pixels (342 ppp) et une haute luminosité : nous l’avons mesurée à 2450 cd/m², soit quasiment au même niveau que l’écran interne de l’appareil. Il concède la même quantité de reflets qu’un écran de smartphone conventionnel (46,34 % de la lumière reçue, d’après nos mesures) : il est toutefois suffisamment lumineux pour être très lisible en extérieur.
Dans la mesure où Samsung a renforcé les usages de cet écran, en facilitant l’accès aux applications du smartphone plutôt qu’à de simples widgets, il pourra être utilisé confortablement pour qui s’accommode de sa petite taille. En revanche, on note que Samsung ne propose pas de réglages d’affichage spécifiques : il faudra donc se contenter de couleurs franchement chaudes (6192,6 K), mais pour un delta E fort bas, à 1,43.
Soyons honnêtes : s’il est possible de regarder/retoucher ses photos ou de visionner des vidéos sur cet écran, il est surtout pratique pour gérer ses notifications et consulter des informations basiques qui ne demandent pas une précision colorimétrique absolue.
Samsung réserve le Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 à ses Galaxy Z Fold 2026. Moins cher, le Galaxy Z Flip 8 doit se contenter de la puce qui anime le Galaxy S26, lui aussi moins bien loti que le Galaxy S26 Ultra, à savoir l’Exynos 2600. Le chipset, gravé en 2 nm, compte dix cœurs CPU, dont un C1-Ultra à 2,8 GHz, trois C1-Pro à 3,25 GHz et six C1-Pro à 2,75 GHz, complétés par un GPU Xclipse 960. Samsung flanque cette puce de 12 Go de RAM, quelle que soit l’option de stockage (256 ou 512 Go) retenue.
Les performances multitâches sont au rendez-vous, et sont à peine moins élevées que celles assurées par la puce Snapdragon. Il n’y a rien à relever de ce côté, et c’est tant mieux : on ne pardonnerait pas un manque de fluidité à un smartphone à son niveau de prix.
Les résultats sont plus contrastés sur le plan des performances graphiques. Le smartphone parvient ainsi à afficher près de 95 i/s de moyenne sur notre test Viser classique, et même 66 i/is au niveau supérieur. Le framerate est certes élevé, mais on constate qu’il manque de stabilité et baisse rapidement lors des utilisations intensives. La faute à une tendance à la chauffe assez prononcée (45 °C ont été relevés sous notre caméra thermique).
Bref, si le smartphone est taillé pour tous types d’applications, on ne peut pas vraiment le conseiller aux amateurs de gaming, qui risquent d’avoir chaud aux mains… et de devoir recharger bien trop vite leur appareil.
On ne peut pas dire que la série Flip fasse sa mue sur le plan de la photographie. Samsung recycle l'équipement de son Z Flip 7, et équipe son modèle 8 d'un double module photo, le premier doté d'un capteur de 50 mégapixels, et le second, de 12 Mpx. Seuls le grand-angle et l'ultra grand-angle sont proposés, le téléobjectif restant aux abonnés absents ; le zoom x2 visible dans l'interface du smartphone correspond en réalité à un grossissement numérique.
Samsung livre des images de 12 mégapixels (il faut pour cela remercier le pixel-binning) de qualité honorable, mais sans doute pas la meilleure de son catalogue. Les images sont détaillées au centre, mais aussi en périphérie, malgré un léger flou sur les pourtours de l'image. Elles sont un peu moins bruitées que ne le sont celles du Galaxy Z Flip 7, et les couleurs sont globalement neutres. On a vu des rendus au piqué plus élevé, mais l'ensemble est harmonieux.
En basse lumière, exercice assez périlleux pour le Galaxy Z Flip 7, le Z Flip 8 limite l'apparition d'artefacts. Le contours ne sont pas suraccentués, mais les textures sont lissées et les contours des petits éléments perdent en précision. Bruité et vignetté, le pourtour de la scène est difficilement exploitable.
Mode 50 mégapixels
Pour le plaisir, voici les clichés que l'on obtient en optant pour le mode 50 mégapixels, aisément accessibles dans les paramètres de l'app Photo. Le mode peut être utile lorsque l'éclairage est généreux, et encore : le traitement perd franchement en naturel.
On remarque d'emblée que Samsung a revu son traitement d'images, du moins en ce qui concerne les couleurs. À l'ultra grand-angle, en pleine lumière, elles sont moins saturées, plus neutres. En revanche, le manque de piqué est visible et les détails manquent de netteté. Comme toujours, la distorsion est efficacement corrigée par le logiciel de la marque, même si le flou l'emporte au fur et à mesure que l'on s'éloigne du centre de l'image.
Changement de cap sur le plan des clichés en basse lumière. À l'ultra grand-angle, le Z Flip 7 tentait le pari de l'accentuation des contours et d'un lissage abusif transformant les textures en aplats de couleurs peu esthétiques. Son successeur lui préfère un bruit qui fait disparaître les détails fins, quitte à brouiller l'ensemble.
Samsung assure toujours le strict minimum pour ce qui concerne les selfies, intégrant un capteur de 10 Mpx à son écran interne. Il a assez peu d'intérêt en soi, puisqu'il paraît bien plus pertinent d'exploiter le module principal du smartphone en utilisant son écran externe comme moniteur à la prise de selfies. Il est d'autant plus utile que le Flex Mode (utilisation du smartphone à demi ouvert) permet de le poser sur une table et d'éviter la sempiternelle image capturée à bout de bras.
Côté vidéo, pas de nouveautés non plus. L'appareil propose au mieux de la 4K à 60 i/s. Pour bénéficier des modes de stabilisation supplémentaires, dont le verrouillage de l'horizon, il faut toutefois se contenter d'un maximum de 30 i/s en 4K. Le mode "Double enregistrement", qui permet de filmer avec deux modules différents au dos et en façade, est également disponible.
Samsung équipe son Galaxy Z Flip 8 d’une batterie de 4300 mAh, c’est-à-dire la même capacité que celle du Z Flip 7. Il intègre néanmoins à son accumulateur une dose de silicium-carbone, ce qui lui permet d’être plus compact que son prédécesseur ; l’ergonomie a donc été privilégiée à la promesse d’une endurance accrue. Ce qui n’est pas spécialement gênant, le Z Flip 7 s’étant montré suffisamment endurant pour convaincre, avec ses 21 h 02 min d’utilisation mesurées sur notre protocole de test Viser habituel. Son successeur assure d’ailleurs une endurance très comparable : nous avons relevé, sur le même test, 20 h 51 min d’usage. Selon que vous utiliserez plus ou moins son Cover Display au quotidien, vous pourrez toutefois prolonger cette durée de quelques heures, l'écran comptant parmi les postes de consommation d'énergie principaux.
Le fabricant a mis un coup d’accélérateur côté charge rapide, du moins pour ses Z Fold : les modèles 8 et 8 Ultra ont droit à une recharge à 45 W. Mais leur compagnon à clapet doit se contenter d’une puissance maintenue à 25 W, toujours légère au regard des standards actuels. Il nous a fallu tout de même 1 h 35 min pour en faire le plein. C’est trop, même si on apprécie la possibilité de faire appel à la charge sans-fil Qi 2 à 15 W. Elle est potentiellement magnétique, si toutefois vous acquérez une coque dotée d’une plaque aimantée pour en profiter.
Notre score de durabilité permet de déterminer l'aspect durable du smartphone, autant pour le consommateur que pour l'environnement. Il s'appuie sur des éléments puisés dans l’étiquette énergie mise en place par l’Union européenne (classe énergétique, scores de résistance aux chutes et de réparabilité, nombre de cycles de batterie avant de tomber sous une capacité de 80 % et résistance de l’écran aux rayures). Nous y ajoutons des critères de durabilité (indice de protection IP, connecteurs standards, durée de garantie et des mises à jour…) et une évaluation des politiques RSE (Responsabilité sociétale des entreprises). Vous trouverez tous les détails de l'analyse dans notre article présentant notre score de durabilité.
Les smartphones pliants à clapet semblent être arrivés à un niveau tel de maturité technique qu'il devient difficile de véritablement innover. Le Galaxy Z Flip 8 de Samsung l'illustre parfaitement. S'il se paie le luxe d'être un peu plus fin et plus léger que son prédécesseur et ose enfin le pari d'une batterie au silicium-carbone, il apporte peu de nouveautés matérielles à sa série. Doté d'écrans toujours aussi lumineux, performant - quoiqu'un peu moins que les Z Fold 8 - et endurant, il pèche toujours par une charge trop peu rapide, et se rattrape par un volet logiciel peaufiné. Dans l'ensemble donc, le smartphone est réussi, mais peine à se distinguer d'un Z Flip 7 qui reste d'actualité.
Nous le précisons plus haut : le principal concurrent du Galaxy Z Flip 8, c'est en réalité son prédécesseur, le Z Flip 7 : il est certes un chouïa plus épais et plus lourd, mais assure une prestation dans l'ensemble équivalente, pour un tarif qui a baissé au fil des mois. Notre meilleur conseil sera donc de guetter les promotions, et d'aller au plus avantageux.

articles.title: « Saturn V était meilleure » : le patron de la NASA flingue 20 ans de choix stratégiques
articles.text:
On a connu des prises de position plus modérées de Jared Isaacman. Dans une longue prise de parole publiée le 9 août, l’administrateur de la NASA a posé un diagnostic public d’une sévérité rare sur l’état de l’agence spatiale américaine. Selon lui, « la NASA ne peut pas réussir si elle essaie de mener en parallèle une infinité de programmes de développement complexes et coûteux. »
Pour l’homme d’affaires, désormais en poste depuis huit mois, vouloir tout faire en interne et en même temps a conduit l’agence à se retrouver dans une impasse. En voulant tout mener de front, l’agence s’est mise à faire des compromis de plus en plus importants afin de tenir ses objectifs, ce qui a eu pour effet de multiplier les retards et les surcoûts.
Saturn V ridiculise le Space Launch System (SLS)
Parmi les victimes de ce grand déballage sur X figurent les deux piliers historiques du programme Artémis, qui consiste à ramener des astronautes sur la Lune. D’abord, le lanceur lourd SLS (Space Launch System). S’il semblait logique en 2005 de vouloir recycler les composants de l’ancienne navette spatiale, le résultat fait aujourd’hui grincer des dents.
Jared Isaacman fait au passage une comparaison cruelle pour le SLS : le mythique lanceur Saturn V des missions Apollo « était matériellement meilleur pour convertir la masse au sol en masse envoyée vers la Lune. » Le SLS, lui, est un gouffre financier, et est rétrogradé au simple rang de solution de transition, en attendant de meilleures fusées.
La station orbitale lunaire (Lunar Gateway) en prend aussi pour son grade, alors que ce devait être un passage intermédiaire (et obligé) pour aller sur la Lune. Décrite comme « indéfiniment suspendue » et accusée de compliquer inutilement la vie du programme Artémis, la station aurait en somme apporté plus de problèmes que de solutions.
En fait, Jared Isaacman résume la nouvelle philosophie ainsi : « Nous voulons construire l’infrastructure pour une présence durable sur un autre monde… pas au-dessus. »
Fini le saupoudrage, place à la « Nuclear NASA »
La stratégie d’externalisation à outrance en prend aussi pour son grade. Le modèle du « tout-commercial » (louer un rover ou un réacteur comme un service, plutôt que de le construire) a surtout servi de cache-misère pour masquer le sous-financement de certains programmes.
À force de boucher les trous avec des partenaires qui ont eux-mêmes des problèmes de budget, « vous n’obtenez rien de ce que vous voulez vraiment sur la Lune parce que vous vous éparpillez trop », a lancé le patron de l’agence, cinglant.
Pourquoi une telle remise en question aujourd’hui ?
Parce que le temps presse. En toile de fond, c’est l’ombre du programme spatial chinois qui dicte ce recadrage d’urgence. Ainsi, Jared Isaacman admet que « la seconde course à l’espace va être beaucoup plus serrée qu’elle ne l’aurait dû ». Car Pékin apparaît encore plus motivé et plus capable que Moscou à l’époque de la guerre froide.
L’heure est donc au pragmatisme pur et dur : réparer le programme SLS, imposer une cadence stricte d’un tir lunaire par an, et surtout, préparer la mutation technologique de l’agence. L’objectif n’est plus seulement de fouler à nouveau la poussière lunaire, mais d’amorcer la transition vers la « Nuclear NASA ».
Maîtriser la propulsion et l’énergie nucléaires est désormais l’urgence absolue pour s’assurer que « la troisième course ne sera jamais remise en question. »
